  • Only ever moves forward — never jumps back
  • Its absolute value is meaningless; comparing it across machines is nonsense
  • NTP may slew its rate (±0.05%) but cannot jump it
  • Use for: timeouts, latency measurement, rate limiters, retry backoff
⚠ Common misconception
“Measuring how long something took with two currentTimeMillis() calls is fine.”

It is fine until NTP steps the clock backwards mid-measurement — and then your duration is negative.

What happens next depends on your code. A negative duration in a retry backoff can produce an immediate infinite retry loop. In a rate limiter it can hand out unlimited tokens. In a lease check it can make an expired lease look valid. The bug lives for months and fires once, during a clock correction, with no way to reproduce it.

Rule: if you are subtracting two timestamps, you want the monotonic clock. Always.

Process Pauses — The Assumption That Breaks Everything

Here is the deepest idea in this chapter, and it is the one that separates people who have read about distributed systems from people who have debugged them.

Consider a leader holding a lease — a lock with a timeout. To stay leader it must renew before expiry. The natural implementation looks obviously correct:

// This code is WRONG. Two separate bugs. while (true) { request = getIncomingRequest(); // keep at least 10s of lease remaining if (lease.expiryTimeMillis - System.currentTimeMillis() < 10000) { lease = lease.renew(); } if (lease.isValid()) { process(request); // <-- what if we pause HERE? } }

Bug one: the expiry time was set by a different machine, and is being compared against this machine's wall clock. If those clocks differ by a few seconds, the logic is already wrong.

Bug two is worse, and no clock fixes it. The code assumes almost no time passes between checking lease.isValid() and running process(request). Normally that is microseconds. But if the thread is paused for 15 seconds right there, the lease expires, another node becomes leader — and this thread has no idea. It wakes up and processes the request as though it were still leader.

WHY A THREAD CAN PAUSE FOR SECONDS OR MINUTES ● Stop-the-world GC. JVM full GC pauses have been observed lasting minutes. Even "concurrent" collectors stop the world sometimes. ● VM suspension. A hypervisor can suspend a VM at any instruction and resume it later — live migration does exactly this. ● Laptop lid. On end-user devices, execution simply stops. ● Context switch / hypervisor steal. A noisy neighbour can starve your vCPU for an unbounded time. ● Swap / page fault. One memory access becomes a disk read. Thrashing turns microseconds into seconds. ● Synchronous disk I/O you did not know was there — classloading, a log write to a full disk, an fsync behind a lock. ● SIGSTOP from an operator, resumed much later with SIGCONT. A node cannot detect its own pause. From inside, no time passed. Only the outside world knows, and it has already moved on.
This is why “check the condition, then act” is unsafe in a distributed system: the gap between the check and the act is unbounded.
💡 The mental model to keep

On a single machine with threads, you protect a critical section with a mutex and the OS guarantees exclusion. In a distributed system there is no such guarantee — a node can be arbitrarily delayed while believing it holds exclusive access, and no amount of checking helps, because the check itself can be stale by the time you act on it.

So the safe pattern is never “check that I still hold the lock.” It is “make it impossible for my write to land if I no longer hold the lock” — enforced by the thing being written to.

Fencing Tokens — The Fix, and It Must Live in the Storage Layer

Here is the corruption in full, and it is not hypothetical — HBase shipped this bug:

WITHOUT FENCING — two clients write, file is corrupted Client 1 acquires lease ────────┦ ├─ GC PAUSE (long) ──────────────┦ │ lease expires... │ Client 2 └─ acquires lease ── writes ─┦ │ Client 1 resumes, still believes it holds the lease, WRITES ↓ FILE CORRUPTED WITH FENCING — the storage layer rejects the stale writer Client 1 acquires lease, token = 33 ──┦ ├─ GC PAUSE ──────────┦ Client 2 acquires lease, token = 34 ── write(token=34) → ACCEPTED storage remembers: max seen = 34 Client 1 resumes ─────────┦ write(token=33) → REJECTED 33 < 34 → stale writer ↓ DATA INTACT. Client 1 learns it lost the lock.
A fencing token is a monotonically increasing number issued with every lock grant. The resource tracks the highest token it has seen and rejects anything lower.
⚠ The part that is most often got wrong

The check must happen at the resource, not at the client. A client verifying its own lock status is worthless — the stale client is the thing that is wrong, and it sincerely believes it is fine.

If your storage does not support fencing natively, you can often smuggle it in: put the token in the filename, in a conditional-write predicate, or in a version column (WHERE epoch <= 34). What you cannot do is skip it and rely on the lock alone.

Where do tokens come from? Any monotonic counter from the coordination service: ZooKeeper's zxid or node cversion, etcd's revision, or Raft's term number — Raft's term is a fencing token by another name.

⚠ Common misconception
“We use a distributed lock, so exactly one process is doing the work.”

A distributed lock guarantees that at most one process believes it holds the lock at any moment. It does not guarantee that at most one process is acting on that belief — because a paused process cannot know its belief expired.

This distinction matters enormously in practice. It is why a lock is fine for efficiency (avoid duplicate work; a duplicate is merely wasteful) and unsafe for correctness (duplicates corrupt data) unless fenced.

Ask yourself this before every distributed lock: if two processes ran this simultaneously, would I lose money or corrupt data, or just waste CPU? If the former, a lock is not enough — you need fencing enforced at the resource.

Clock Readings Have a Confidence Interval

The most useful reframing in this chapter: a timestamp is not a point, it is a range. Your clock reads 10:00:00.123, but given drift since the last NTP sync and the network delay in that sync, the true time is somewhere in a window — perhaps 100ms wide on a normal server.

Most APIs hide this and hand you a single number, which invites you to compare timestamps as though they were exact. Google's TrueTime does the opposite — it returns [earliest, latest] and forces you to confront the uncertainty. That honesty is what makes Spanner's ordering guarantee possible:

TWO TIMESTAMPS, ORDER UNKNOWN A: [──────────] confidence interval of A B: [──────────] confidence interval of B ↑ OVERLAP → you CANNOT say A happened before B SPANNER'S ANSWER: make the overlap impossible by WAITING commit at timestamp T A: [──────────] ├─ commit-wait (~2ε, about 7–14ms) ─┦ B: [──────────] ↑ no overlap → B is definitely after A Spanner does not eliminate clock uncertainty. It bounds it, then waits it out. That deliberate wait is a real part of Spanner's write latency.
✎ Mini exercise 5

A nightly billing job must run exactly once. It runs on 5 replicas for availability. You implement it with Redis: SET billing:lock <uuid> NX PX 600000 (10-minute TTL). Whichever replica wins runs the job.

One night, two customers are charged twice. Redis never went down and the logs show only one SET succeeded.

Work out: how this happened despite the lock, and what you would change.

Show the worked answer

What happened: replica A won the lock and started the job. Partway through, it experienced a pause longer than 10 minutes — a stop-the-world GC on a large heap, a VM live-migration, or swap thrashing. Its lock expired. Replica B acquired the lock legitimately and ran the job. Replica A then resumed, unaware that any time had passed, and continued charging customers from where it left off.

Only one SET succeeded at a time — the logs are telling the truth. The lock was never violated. The lock did its job; the lock was simply never sufficient.

What I would change, in order of importance:

  • Make the charge idempotent. Every charge carries an idempotency key like charge:{customer_id}:{billing_period}, enforced by a unique constraint in the ledger. Now a duplicate attempt is rejected by the database regardless of what the lock did. This alone fixes the incident.
  • Add a fencing token. Move the lock to etcd or ZooKeeper, take the revision/zxid as a token, and have the ledger reject writes carrying a token below the highest it has seen. This closes the general case, not just charges.
  • Do not raise the TTL. The instinct is to change 10 minutes to 60. That does not fix anything — it just makes the failure rarer and the recovery slower. There is no TTL that is provably longer than the longest possible pause.

The transferable lesson — and it is the single most valuable one in this chapter: do not try to prevent the stale actor from acting. You cannot. Make its action harmless when it arrives. Idempotency and fencing are both instances of that principle.

🎓 Understanding Check — Time, Pauses and Truth

Teaching questions with answers supplied.
Why does a timeout not tell you whether the server processed your request?

Because a timeout is the absence of a response, and there are at least four ways to get that: the request never arrived; it arrived and is still executing; it executed and the response was lost; or the server crashed midway. All four look identical from the client.

This is why the correct response to a timeout is never simply “retry.” It is “retry an operation I have made safe to repeat” — or query by idempotency key to discover what actually happened.

Why can't a node detect its own pause and refuse to act?

Because from inside the process, no time passed — the pause happens between two instructions and leaves no trace in the program's own state. The thread resumes exactly where it left off with all its assumptions intact.

It could re-read the clock after resuming and notice a large jump — and defensive code sometimes does this. But it is fundamentally a race: the check happens after resuming, and the unsafe action may already be in flight. The reliable fix is external enforcement (fencing), not internal detection.

Why is “the truth is defined by the majority” the only workable rule?

Because no individual node's view can be trusted — a node may be partitioned, paused, or simply wrong about its own status, and it cannot tell the difference. If any single node's belief counted, a partitioned node would keep acting as leader.

A quorum works because two majorities of the same set must overlap in at least one member, and that member carries the memory of the earlier decision. So a node that lost its majority genuinely has lost its authority, whatever it believes.

When are synchronized clocks actually safe to rely on?

When you either (a) only need approximate answers — log timestamps, metric buckets, cache TTLs where a few seconds of error is harmless; or (b) explicitly account for the uncertainty, as Spanner does with confidence intervals and commit-wait.

They are not safe for ordering events across machines when correctness depends on the order. Last-write-wins conflict resolution is the canonical misuse: a node with a fast clock can silently suppress every correct write from its peers for the duration of the skew.

What is the practical difference between a lock used for efficiency and one used for correctness?

An efficiency lock prevents duplicate work; if it occasionally fails, you waste CPU. Redis SET NX PX is entirely adequate here.

A correctness lock prevents data corruption; if it fails, you lose money or destroy data. This needs a consensus-backed lock service plus fencing enforced at the resource — and ideally an idempotent operation underneath so the lock is a performance optimisation rather than the safety mechanism.

Asking which kind you have, out loud, before writing the code, prevents a whole class of production incident.

🌱 Takeaway — Time and Truth

This chapter is about a single uncomfortable fact: you cannot trust your own clock, your own liveness, or your own beliefs about your role.

  • Two clocks. Monotonic for durations, wall clock for calendar times. Subtracting wall-clock timestamps is a bug waiting for an NTP correction.
  • Processes pause arbitrarily — GC, VM migration, swap, hypervisor steal. There is no safe upper bound, so no TTL is provably long enough.
  • A node cannot detect its own pause. Any “check then act” has an unbounded gap between the check and the act.
  • Fencing tokens are the fix, and they must be enforced at the resource. Client-side checking is worthless.
  • Timestamps are intervals, not points. If the intervals overlap, the order is unknown — and pretending otherwise is how LWW loses data.
  • Truth is whatever a quorum agrees on, never what one node believes.

Which raises the question the next chapters answer: how does a group of nodes agree on anything at all, when none of them can be trusted individually? That is consensus.

📝 Interview Q&A

Your team is debating whether to use timestamps or version numbers for conflict detection. How do you advise?

Version numbers (monotonic integers) for conflict detection; timestamps for human-readable ordering.

Timestamps fail for conflict detection because of clock skew. If Server A updates with ts=1000 and Server B updates with ts=999 (B's clock is slightly behind), LWW would choose A's write even if B's write came later in real time. You've silently lost data.

Version numbers (also called sequence numbers or ETags in HTTP) are safe: compare expected_version with current_version. If they match, proceed. If not, conflict detected. No clock dependence.

In practice: use optimistic locking with version numbers for conflict detection. Use timestamps only for things like 'when was this created' (human display), not for deciding which write wins.

Explain why vector clocks are better than Lamport clocks for detecting write conflicts in a distributed database.

Lamport clocks provide a total order — every event gets a number and A < B means A happened before B. But if A has Lamport clock 5 and B has clock 8, you cannot tell if A caused B or if they're concurrent. 8 > 5 just means B happened after A OR at the same time with a different process sequence.

Vector clocks provide partial order with concurrency detection. If VC_A = [2, 0, 0] and VC_B = [0, 2, 0], neither dominates the other — they're concurrent writes. Both happened without knowledge of the other. This is exactly when you have a conflict to resolve.

For a database, concurrent writes to the same key need to be resolved (LWW, app merge, or surfaced to user). Lamport clocks would silently discard one. Vector clocks let you detect and handle the conflict correctly.

Chapter 9
Caching
The most impactful single optimization in distributed systems — and the hardest to get right.

Caches are everywhere. Your browser caches HTML. Your OS caches disk reads. Your database keeps hot rows in memory. Caching works because of the principle of locality: a small fraction of your data accounts for the vast majority of your access. In web systems, 80% of reads often hit 20% of the data (Pareto principle). Cache that 20% and you serve 80% of traffic from fast memory instead of slow disk or expensive computation.

📖 Analogy

Imagine a librarian who remembers where the 50 most-requested books are, so they can fetch them in 5 seconds instead of 30. The library has 100,000 books but 80% of requests are for the same 50. The librarian's memory is the cache.

Caching Patterns — Which One to Use?

There are four fundamental caching patterns. The wrong choice leads to either stale data or missed optimization opportunities.

The four caching patterns. Cache-aside is the most common and most flexible.

Eviction Policies

Caches have finite memory. When full, they must evict. The right policy depends on your access pattern:

PolicyWhat It DoesBest ForReal Use
LRU (Least Recently Used)Evict the item not accessed for the longest timeTemporal locality — recent = relevantRedis default, most web caches
LFU (Least Frequently Used)Evict the item accessed fewest timesStable access patterns (top-N always hot)CDN content, video recommendations
FIFO (First In, First Out)Evict oldest inserted itemSimple, predictableLow-priority queues, simple buffers
TTL (Time To Live)Evict after a set time regardless of accessData that expires naturally (tokens, sessions)Session caches, auth tokens
SLRU (Segmented LRU)Protected + probationary segmentsHigh churn with some always-hot itemsDatabase buffer pools (InnoDB)

Cache Problems You Must Know

1. Thundering Herd (Cache Stampede)

A popular cache entry expires. At the exact moment it expires, 1,000 concurrent requests come in. All miss. All query the DB simultaneously. The DB dies.

🎯 Scenario — The Frontend Stampede

Your homepage loads user recommendations from a Redis cache with a 10-minute TTL. At 9:00:00 AM, the cache expires for user ID 1 (celebrity account with 10M followers). In the next 200ms, 5,000 requests arrive for user 1's recommendations. All miss. All 5,000 hit the DB. DB query time: 500ms. You just sent 5,000 concurrent 500ms queries to a DB expecting 100 QPS.

Solutions:

  • Mutex/Singleflight: Only one goroutine fetches from DB. Others wait for the result. When the first returns, all get it.
  • Probabilistic Early Recomputation: Before TTL expires, with increasing probability, recompute in the background. XFetch algorithm.
  • Stale-while-revalidate: Serve the stale value. Trigger an async refresh. No blocking.
  • Jittered TTLs: Instead of TTL=600s for all users, use TTL=600 + random(0,60). Distributes expirations over time.

2. Cache Penetration

Requests for keys that don't exist — either in cache or DB. With cache-aside, every request for a non-existent key goes to the DB. An attacker can spam random non-existent IDs and hammer your DB.

Solution: Cache null results with a short TTL (e.g., 5 min). 'Key not found' → store NULL → subsequent requests return NULL from cache. Alternatively: Bloom filter to check existence before any lookup.

3. Cache Avalanche

Many cache entries expire at the same time (e.g., after a cache server restart). Traffic floods the DB.

Solutions: Jitter TTLs (different expiries). Redis Cluster (no single cache server restart loses all data). Pre-warming: populate cache from DB before routing traffic.

💡 Key Insight

Cache hit rate is your most important cache metric. A 99% hit rate means 1% of traffic hits the DB. A 95% hit rate means 5× more DB traffic — which at high QPS can be the difference between a healthy system and an outage.

Multi-Layer Caching (L1/L2/L3)

Production systems use multiple cache layers. Facebook's Memcache paper introduced the 'look-aside cache' at scale:

LayerWhereLatencyHit Rate Target
L1: In-processLocal memory in the app server~1μs30-40%
L2: Local cacheRedis/Memcache on same host~100μs50-70%
L3: Distributed cacheRedis Cluster across many machines~1ms90-99%
L4: CDNEdge servers globally~10ms80-95% for static
L5: Origin/DBDatabase~10msLast resort
🔬 Google-Level Depth — Facebook's Memcache at Scale

Facebook (2013 paper) runs thousands of Memcache servers globally. Key engineering choices:

  • Lease mechanism: When a key is deleted/invalidated, a lease token is issued. Only the token holder can refill that key. Others wait. Prevents stampede AND resolves stale-set races.
  • Regional pools: Wildcard pool (all data) + specialized pools for hot keys. Hot keys replicated to many more servers.
  • Invalidation pipeline: DB → MySQL binlog → McSqueal (invalidation daemon) → all Memcache servers. Ensures no stale data after DB writes.
  • Thundering herd: 'Staggered restarts' — never restart all cache servers simultaneously. Gradual rollout prevents cold-cache flood.

📝 Interview Q&A

Your Redis cache has a 95% hit rate. Is that good?

It depends entirely on your DB capacity. 95% sounds high, but:

If you're handling 100K QPS: 5% miss = 5,000 QPS to the DB. If your DB handles 10K QPS, you're 50% over capacity — that's a crisis.

At 99% hit rate: 1,000 QPS to DB — manageable.

Staff answer: Never evaluate cache hit rate in isolation. Always compute: miss rate × total QPS = DB QPS from cache misses and compare against DB capacity. Also break down hit rates by key type — a 99% hit rate with one hot key type masking a 70% hit rate on another type can hide a ticking time bomb.

How would you implement a distributed cache with cache invalidation across multiple app servers?

Cache invalidation is one of the two hard problems in CS (the other being naming things and off-by-one errors).

Three main strategies:

1. TTL-based (simplest): Let cache entries expire. Stale data for up to TTL duration. Acceptable for low-consistency needs. No active invalidation logic.

2. Event-driven invalidation: After every DB write, publish an invalidation event to a message queue (Kafka/Redis pub/sub). All cache nodes subscribe and delete the key. Challenge: what if a cache node misses the event? Use TTL as a safety net.

3. Write-through invalidation (strongest): Every write goes through a cache layer that atomically updates cache and DB. No stale windows. Cost: write latency. Used by write-heavy, consistency-critical systems.

🎯 Practice Design

Design a CDN with Smart Cache Invalidation

You're building a CDN for a news website. Articles are cached at 200 edge locations globally. When an editor updates an article, the old version must be invalidated across all edges within 10 seconds. Design the cache invalidation system.

Hint areas to cover:
  • How do you propagate invalidation to 200 edge locations within 10 seconds?
  • What data structure do you use at each edge to track cached URLs?
  • How do you handle an edge that's down during invalidation?
  • How do you handle partial invalidation (only some edges cleared) during a network partition?
  • What's your fallback if invalidation fails? (Hint: TTL as safety net)
  • Trade-off: tag-based invalidation vs URL-by-URL invalidation
🔗
Before this section, hold on to three things. From Ch 2: a consistency model is a statement about which orderings of operations are observable. From Ch 4: a replica is a second copy of data that must somehow be kept in agreement with the first. From Ch 5: partitioning breaks a workload into independent pieces so that no single machine sees all of it. A cache is all three at once, which is why it is more dangerous than it looks.

What a Cache Actually Is — A Replica You Have Decided Not to Keep Consistent

The usual framing is that a cache is a performance optimisation. That framing is what makes caching bugs so surprising when they arrive, because it hides the actual decision you made.

Here is the more useful framing. A cache is a replica. It is a second copy of data living somewhere other than the system of record. Chapter 4 spent a long time on the problem of keeping replicas in agreement, and every mechanism it described — synchronous replication, consensus, quorums — costs latency. A cache is what you get when you look at that price list and say: I am not paying it. I will hold a second copy and I will accept that it can be wrong.

That is a legitimate and extremely common engineering decision. But notice what it means: you have not avoided the replication problem. You have chosen a point on the consistency spectrum from Chapter 2, usually without writing it down, and the point you chose is somewhere below eventual consistency — because unlike a real replica, a cache entry with a TTL has no anti-entropy process that will eventually reconcile it. It just sits there being wrong until it expires.

THE STALENESS WINDOW — what a TTL actually promises t=0 read miss -- value V1 loaded into cache, TTL 60s t=5 read hit -- V1 correct t=12 WRITE to database: V1 -> V2 t=13 read hit -- V1 WRONG t=40 read hit -- V1 WRONG t=60 entry expires t=61 read miss -- V2 loaded correct again The window of wrongness is 48 seconds, not 60. It runs from the write to the expiry -- so it depends on WHEN the write lands inside the TTL, which you do not control. "TTL 60s" means "stale for a uniformly random duration between 0 and 60 seconds", averaging 30.
A TTL is not a staleness bound you chose. It is the maximum of a distribution whose mean is half of it, and the tail matters more than the mean when the stale value is a permission, a price, or a feature flag.
⚠ Common misconception
“We set a 60-second TTL, so our data is at most 60 seconds old.”

True, and almost never the thing you actually care about. The question is not how old the data is, it is how long a wrong answer stays observable after the moment it became wrong — and those are different quantities.

Worse, the sentence quietly assumes there is one cache. With an L1 in-process cache in front of an L2 Redis tier, staleness composes: a 10-second local TTL in front of a 60-second shared TTL gives you a worst case of 70 seconds, not 60. Every layer you add multiplies the number of places a stale value can hide, and the layers do not expire in a coordinated way.

The honest version of the sentence is: “a value can be observed up to 70 seconds after it stopped being true, and I have decided that is acceptable for this field.” Say it that way and you will immediately notice the fields for which it is not acceptable.

Hit-Rate Arithmetic — Why 95% and 99% Are Completely Different Systems

Cache hit rate is reported as a percentage, which is exactly the wrong unit for reasoning about it, because the thing you care about is the miss rate and the miss rate is what hits your database. Percentages hide that the interesting scale is multiplicative.

Take 100,000 read QPS at the cache. At a 99% hit rate, 1,000 QPS reach the database. At 95%, 5,000 QPS do. A four-point drop in a number you were monitoring as “still above 95, looks fine” is a 5× increase in database load. At 90% it is 10×. This is the single most important number in cache operations and it is the one most dashboards are designed to obscure.

MISS RATE IS THE LOAD MULTIPLIER, AND IT IS NOT LINEAR hit rate misses/sec DB load vs. the 99% case -------- ---------- ------------------------ 99.9% 100 0.1x 99% 1,000 1x (baseline) 98% 2,000 2x 95% 5,000 5x 90% 10,000 10x 80% 20,000 20x Provision the database for the hit rate you will have during an INCIDENT, not the one on your dashboard today. A cold cache is a 0% hit rate, and that is the load your database sees the moment the cache tier restarts.
The practical consequence: your database capacity plan is really a bet on your cache hit rate holding. If the database cannot survive a cold cache at all, you do not have a cache in front of a database — you have a database whose availability is a function of Redis.
✎ Mini exercise 13

A read path serves 200,000 QPS from Redis at a 98% hit rate. The origin database is provisioned for 12,000 QPS and currently sees 4,000. You are asked to approve a change that adds a new, rarely-read field to the cached object, roughly doubling the number of distinct keys while the Redis memory budget stays fixed.

Work out: what happens, whether the database survives it, and what you should ask for instead.

Show the worked answer

Doubling the key count at a fixed memory budget halves the fraction of the working set you can hold. The exact new hit rate depends on the access distribution, but the direction is certain and the magnitude is usually brutal. If the workload is Zipfian — and read workloads almost always are — you keep most of the hits because the hot keys still fit, so the hit rate might fall from 98% to roughly 94–96% rather than to 49%. That sounds survivable. It is not.

At 98%, misses are 4,000 QPS — matching the observed database load. At 95%, misses are 10,000 QPS. At 94%, 12,000 QPS — exactly the provisioned ceiling, with zero headroom and no allowance for the retry traffic that arrives the moment latency rises. A change described in the review as “adding a small field” has consumed the entire capacity margin of a different team's database.

What to ask for instead. The real error is that one cache entry is serving two access patterns with different temperatures. Split them: keep the hot object cached as it is, and put the rarely-read field in a second key fetched only when needed. Cold data does not belong in the same entry as hot data, because eviction operates on entries and cannot see that only part of the entry is valuable.

The transferable principle: a cache is a fixed-size budget, so every new thing you cache is implicitly a proposal to evict something else. The question is never “should we cache this?” in isolation — it is “what should this displace, and is that trade good?” This is the same reasoning as Chapter 5's hot-partition analysis: a shared fixed resource makes every local decision a global one. It recurs in Chapter 10, where one caller's retry budget is spent out of the same pool as everyone else's.

The Stampede Is a Coordination Problem, and the Fix Is to Coordinate Less

Chapter 9 already introduced the thundering herd. It is worth revisiting because the standard fixes are usually ranked in the wrong order, and because the right one is an instance of the spine that runs through this whole guide.

The mechanism: one popular key expires. In the microsecond after expiry, every concurrent request for that key misses simultaneously, and all of them go to the database to recompute the same value. A key served at 10,000 QPS behind a 50 ms recomputation generates roughly 500 simultaneous identical database queries at the instant it expires. The database does 500 times the necessary work, gets slower, which lengthens the recomputation window, which lets more requests pile in. That is a positive feedback loop, and it is why stampedes look like cliffs rather than bumps.

Three fixes are commonly offered, and they are not equally good:

  • TTL jitter — expire at 60s ± rand(10s) instead of exactly 60s. This is genuinely useful but it solves a different problem: it stops many different keys from expiring at the same instant (the avalanche). It does nothing for a single hot key, because a single key has a single expiry no matter how you jitter it.
  • Early recomputation — probabilistically refresh a key as it approaches expiry, so it is usually renewed before anyone misses. Effective, and elegant, but it is a heuristic: it reduces the probability of a stampede without bounding it.
  • Request coalescing — on a miss, the first request takes a lock and recomputes; every other request for the same key waits for that one result. This is the right answer, because it does not reduce the odds of the herd, it makes the herd structurally impossible. N concurrent misses produce exactly one database query, by construction, regardless of N.
COALESCING: N MISSES BECOME ONE QUERY WITHOUT WITH COALESCING req 1 -- miss --> DB req 1 -- miss --> wins lock --> DB req 2 -- miss --> DB req 2 -- miss --> waits req 3 -- miss --> DB req 3 -- miss --> waits ... ... req 500 - miss --> DB req 500 - miss --> waits | 500 identical queries 1 query, result fanned out to 500 The lock is per-key and held for the recompute duration only. Note the trade you just made: 499 requests now have a LATENCY dependency on one request. If the lock holder hangs, they all hang -- so the wait needs a timeout, and the timeout needs a fallback (serve stale, or fail open).
You have converted a load problem into a latency-coupling problem. That is nearly always the right direction — load problems cascade and latency problems are local — but it is a trade, not a free win, and an interviewer will want to hear you say so.
⚠ Common misconception
“We added a cache, so the system is faster.”

You added a distributed system. The median request got faster; that part is real. But you also acquired: a new failure domain that can be unavailable, a new consistency model nobody wrote down, a capacity plan that now depends on a hit rate, a cold-start problem, a stampede risk, and an entire class of bug where the system misbehaves only for the users whose key happens to be cached.

The p50 improved. The p99 usually got worse, because the p99 request is the one that missed the cache and now pays the cache round trip plus the database round trip. If you are measuring cache success by average latency, you are measuring the half of the distribution that was never the problem.

Cache Penetration — When the Miss Is the Attack

Penetration is the case where the requested key does not exist in the database at all. The cache misses (nothing to cache), the database is queried, the database returns nothing, and so nothing is cached — which means the next identical request repeats the whole journey. Every request for a non-existent key is a guaranteed database hit. An attacker who requests /user/-1, /user/-2, /user/-3 in a loop has a direct, unthrottled channel to your database that your cache is powerless to intercept.

Two defences, and they compose well:

  • Negative caching — cache the absence. Store a tombstone for “this key does not exist” with a short TTL, typically much shorter than the positive TTL, because a key that starts existing should become visible quickly. The short TTL is what bounds the damage of caching a “no” that was only temporarily true.
  • A Bloom filter in front — a probabilistic set membership structure that answers “definitely not present” or “possibly present”. Its one-sided error is exactly the right shape here: a false positive costs you one wasted lookup, and a false negative is impossible, so you can never wrongly reject a key that does exist. Roughly 10 bits per key gives about a 1% false positive rate, so a filter covering 100 million keys fits in about 120 MB — small enough to hold in process, in front of the cache.

🧠 Checking your understanding — Caching

Answers supplied. These are the questions a staff interviewer uses to find out whether you understand caching or have only operated one.
Why is cache invalidation genuinely hard, rather than just annoying?
Because it is a distributed agreement problem wearing a small hat. To invalidate correctly you must ensure that every copy, in every layer, on every node, has dropped the value before any reader can observe the new one. That is a coordination problem across an unreliable network — the same problem Chapter 6 needed consensus for. Most systems dodge it rather than solve it, using TTLs to make wrongness self-healing instead of preventing it. The dodge is correct engineering. It just should be a stated decision, not an accident.
Should you update the cache on write, or delete the entry?
Delete, almost always. Updating writes a value into the cache that you computed at write time, which introduces a race: two concurrent writers can interleave their cache updates in the opposite order to their database writes, leaving the cache permanently holding the older value with no expiry to save you. Deleting has no such race — the worst outcome is an extra miss. Deleting also avoids caching values nobody will read, which is a real cost under a fixed memory budget. The exception is a very hot key with an expensive recompute, where the miss you save is worth the race you must then handle explicitly.
What is the actual difference between write-through and write-back?
Write-through updates cache and database synchronously, so the write is durable when it returns and the cache is never ahead of the database. Write-back updates only the cache and flushes to the database later, which is dramatically faster for write-heavy workloads and means an acknowledged write can be lost if the cache node dies before the flush. That is not a caching nuance, it is a durability decision: write-back turns your cache into the system of record for a window of time. It is the correct choice for view counters and telemetry, and a serious mistake for anything a user would notice losing.
Why is LRU so dominant, given that it is obviously not optimal?
Because it is a good approximation of the optimal policy under the access patterns real systems actually have, and it is cheap. The optimal policy (Bélády's) requires knowing the future. LRU approximates it by assuming recency predicts reuse, which holds for Zipfian workloads — and almost all human-driven workloads are Zipfian. Its famous failure is the sequential scan: one full table scan touches every key once, evicting your entire hot set in favour of data nobody will read again. This is why production systems use LRU variants — segmented LRU, or LFU-with-decay as in Redis's allkeys-lfu — that require a key to be touched more than once before it can displace established residents.
Your cache tier goes down entirely. What happens, and what should happen?
What happens by default: 100% of read traffic arrives at a database provisioned for the miss rate, which is 20× to 100× over capacity. The database saturates, latency rises, clients time out and retry, and the retries add load — a metastable failure that will not recover on its own even after the cache returns, because the retry backlog keeps the database saturated. What should happen: the cache client must fail open with a concurrency limit to the database rather than an unbounded pass-through, shedding load beyond it. Serving 15% of users correctly and rejecting 85% quickly is a far better outcome than serving 0% because everything is timing out. This is Chapter 10's material and it is the reason caching and load shedding cannot be designed separately.
When should you not use a cache at all?
When the read-to-write ratio is near 1, because you will pay the invalidation cost on every write and get almost no hits in return. When the working set exceeds the cache by a wide margin and access is uniform rather than Zipfian, because you will thrash and pay the cache round trip on top of every database round trip for a hit rate near zero. And when a stale read is genuinely unacceptable — authorisation decisions, account balances, anything where being wrong for 30 seconds is a security or financial incident. In that last case the answer is not a shorter TTL; it is that the cache must be on the write path or absent, because a TTL is a bound on wrongness, never an elimination of it.
🎯 Which caching choice real systems make, and why
CDN / static assets
Long TTL plus content-hashed URLs. The trick is that the URL changes when the content does, so invalidation is never needed — a new version is simply a different key. This is the strongest available answer and it works whenever you control the URL.
Social feed / timeline
Cache-aside with a generous TTL. Staleness is invisible to users because there is no ground truth they can compare against — nobody knows which post should have been at the top. Ch 4
Session / auth tokens
Short TTL and an explicit revocation channel. This is the case where TTL alone is insufficient: logout must take effect now, so revocation is pushed rather than waited out.
Product price / inventory
Very short TTL or write-through. Showing a stale price is a commercial and sometimes legal problem, so this is a case where the cache is on the write path.
View counters / telemetry
Write-back, batched. Losing 30 seconds of counts on a node failure is acceptable; taking a database write per view is not. An explicit durability trade made in favour of throughput.
Feature flags / config
Long TTL with push invalidation, and a local in-process cache so the flag check never blocks on the network. The failure mode that matters is not staleness, it is a flag service outage taking down every caller that depends on it.
🌱 Takeaway — Caching

A cache is a replica you have chosen not to keep consistent. Everything difficult about caching follows from that one sentence.

  • Name the staleness you accepted. “TTL 60s” is a mechanism; “a wrong answer stays observable for up to 70 seconds across both layers” is the decision.
  • Miss rate is the load multiplier, and it is multiplicative. 99% → 95% is 5× the database load. Capacity-plan for the hit rate you will have in an incident, which is zero.
  • Coalesce rather than jitter for a single hot key. Jitter reduces probability; coalescing makes the herd structurally impossible. You pay in latency coupling, which is the cheaper currency.
  • Delete on write, do not update. Updating buys you one avoided miss and sells you a permanent-staleness race.
  • Cache the absence too. Otherwise every request for a key that does not exist is an unthrottled path to your database.
  • Design the cache-down case explicitly. If a cache outage takes the database with it, the cache is not an optimisation — it is a hard dependency you have not admitted to.

Chapter 10 picks up exactly where the last point leaves off: once you accept that your origin can be overwhelmed, the question becomes how to distribute what arrives and how to refuse what you cannot serve.

Chapter 10
Load Balancing & Rate Limiting
Distributing traffic intelligently — and protecting your system from being overwhelmed.

Load balancing is the practice of distributing incoming requests across multiple servers. Without it, all traffic hits one server, which both limits your scale and creates a single point of failure.

Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing

The biggest architectural decision in load balancing is which layer to operate at:

L4 vs L7 load balancing. Most production systems use both: L4 for the outer tier, L7 for service-level routing.

Load Balancing Algorithms

AlgorithmLogicBest ForProblem
Round RobinRequests cycle: 1→2→3→1→2→3Uniform request costServer 2 might be slow; still gets equal load
Least ConnectionsSend to server with fewest active connectionsVariable request durationRequires tracking state across all backends
Least Response TimeCombine: fewest connections + lowest latencyHeterogeneous serversMore complex, requires active monitoring
Consistent HashingHash(user/session) → always same backendStateful servers (WebSocket, sessions)Uneven distribution if few servers
Random with Two Choices (P2C)Pick 2 random backends, send to better oneLarge clusters (O(1) overhead)Slightly suboptimal vs least-connections
💡 Key Insight

Power of Two Random Choices (P2C) is the secret weapon for large-scale LB. Instead of checking all N backends (O(N)) or maintaining sorted order, pick 2 at random and use the better one. Achieves near-optimal distribution with O(1) overhead. Used by Nginx, Envoy, and Netflix's Ribbon.

Rate Limiting — The Circuit Breaker for Traffic

Rate limiting protects your system from overwhelming traffic — whether from bugs, abusive clients, or traffic spikes. Without it, one misbehaving client can take down your system for everyone.

Token Bucket Algorithm (Most Common)

Imagine a bucket that holds tokens. Tokens are added at a fixed rate (e.g., 100/sec). Each request consumes one token. When the bucket is empty, requests are rejected. The bucket has a maximum size (burst capacity).

Token bucket: allows bursting up to bucket capacity, then smooths to the refill rate.

Sliding Window Rate Limiting

Token bucket allows bursty behavior. Sliding window is more precise: count requests in the last N seconds. If count ≥ limit, reject.

Implementation: For each user, maintain a Redis sorted set with timestamps as scores. On each request: ZADD user:requests timestamp timestamp. Then ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to remove entries older than the window. Then ZCARD to count. If count ≥ limit → reject.

Distributed Rate Limiting

Per-node rate limiting is easy but inaccurate. If you have 10 app servers each with a 100 req/sec limit, a user can send 1000 req/sec by round-robining across servers.

Options: (1) Centralized rate limiter (Redis) — authoritative but adds latency. (2) Token bucket with gossip — each node tracks locally, periodically syncs with others. Slightly over-allows (~10%) but fast. (3) Sticky routing — consistent hash by user ID, so each user's requests always go to the same server.

📝 Interview Q&A

Design a rate limiter for a public API: 1000 req/min per API key. 10M API keys. What are your considerations?

Storage: 10M keys × ~100 bytes per key (counter + timestamp) = 1 GB. Fits in Redis. Use Redis hashes per API key.

Algorithm: Token bucket for burst-friendliness, or sliding window for precision. Sliding window requires per-request sorted set update — O(log N) per request.

Distributed: Single Redis node is a SPOF. Redis Cluster with consistent hashing on API key. Each key is handled by one shard (no cross-shard coordination).

Fault tolerance: If Redis is down: fail open (allow requests) or fail closed (deny requests). Usually fail open — don't make your API entirely unavailable because the rate limiter is down.

Response headers: Return X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, Retry-After for good DX.

🎯 Practice Design

Design a Rate Limiter for a Payments API

You're building a payments API used by 50,000 merchants. Each merchant gets 100 requests/minute. Some merchants are enterprise tier with 10,000 requests/minute. Design the rate limiting system.

Hint areas to cover:
  • How do you store per-merchant state at scale?
  • How do you handle tiered limits (standard vs enterprise)?
  • What happens when your rate limiter (Redis) goes down? Fail open or closed?
  • How do you prevent a merchant from circumventing limits by using multiple IPs?
  • How do you implement a 'daily quota' (10,000 total/day) in addition to per-minute rate?
  • What metrics do you expose to merchants about their rate limit status?
🔗
Two things carry over. From Ch 1: you cannot distinguish a slow node from a dead one, so every routing decision is made on stale information about backend health. From Ch 9: your origin's capacity plan is a bet on a cache hit rate, so the load arriving here is far more variable than the request rate suggests.

Load Balancing Is a Queueing Problem, Not a Distribution Problem

The word “balancing” is misleading. It suggests the goal is to give each backend an equal number of requests, and that is not the goal — it is a proxy for the goal, and a surprisingly poor one. What you actually want to minimise is the maximum queue depth across the fleet, because the slowest backend is what your p99 is made of.

Those two objectives diverge the moment requests cost different amounts, which is always. If one request in a hundred takes 500 ms and the rest take 5 ms, then handing every backend the same count of requests hands them wildly different amounts of work. Round robin is optimal for a workload nobody has.

The obvious fix is least-connections: send each request to whichever backend currently has the fewest in flight. This genuinely tracks load rather than count. Its problem is that it requires global state — every load balancer must know every backend's current depth — and maintaining that across a fleet of load balancers is both expensive and, per Chapter 1, always slightly wrong. Worse, when several load balancers independently observe that backend 7 is least loaded, they all send it their next request simultaneously. The information was true when they read it and false by the time they acted on it. This is herd behaviour caused by accurate monitoring, and it is a genuinely counter-intuitive failure.

The Power of Two Choices — The Best Return on One Extra Probe in All of Systems

Here is the result, and it is one of the most useful things in this chapter. Suppose you place n requests onto n backends.

  • Choose each backend purely at random: the most-loaded backend ends up with about log n / log log n requests. At n = 1,000 that is roughly 5.
  • Sample two backends at random and pick the less loaded of the two: the most-loaded backend ends up with about log log n requests. At n = 1,000 that is roughly 3.

That does not sound dramatic until you notice it is an exponential improvement in the tail, and that it costs one additional probe and no shared state whatsoever. Going from two choices to three buys you almost nothing more; essentially the entire benefit arrives with the second sample. This is why power of two choices (P2C) is the default in modern proxies — it captures nearly all of the benefit of least-connections while remaining fully decentralised, which also means it cannot produce the herd effect that global least-connections does.

POWER OF TWO CHOICES -- why one extra probe collapses the tail PURE RANDOM TWO CHOICES pick 1 backend at random pick 2 at random, send to the shallower b1 [## ] 2 b1 [## ] 2 b2 [###### ] 6 <-- tail b2 [### ] 3 b3 [# ] 1 b3 [## ] 2 b4 [#### ] 4 b4 [### ] 3 <-- tail max load ~ log n / log log n max load ~ log log n n=1000 -> ~5 n=1000 -> ~3 No shared state. No coordination. Each load balancer decides alone, and because it decides alone it cannot stampede the same "least loaded" backend that every other load balancer just observed. Global knowledge would be MORE accurate and produce WORSE outcomes.
This is the guide's recurring spine in its purest form: make the decision local instead of coordinating. It appeared in Ch 4 as partitioning by conversation, in Ch 6 as keeping the balance on one shard, in Ch 7 as moving the invariant onto one row. Here, a deliberately incomplete local view beats a complete global one.
⚠ Common misconception
“Round robin distributes load evenly across the backends.”

Round robin distributes requests evenly. Load is requests multiplied by cost, and request cost in any real service varies by one or two orders of magnitude — a cache hit versus a cache miss, a user with 3 followers versus one with 3 million.

The failure mode is specific and worth being able to name: a backend that receives an unlucky run of expensive requests slows down, its queue grows, and round robin keeps sending it requests at exactly the same rate, because round robin has no feedback channel. A struggling backend is given precisely as much work as a healthy one until it fails outright. Least-connections and P2C both have this feedback implicitly — a backend with a deep queue is visibly deep — which is the real reason to prefer them, ahead of any argument about statistical evenness.

Distributed Rate Limiting — Where the Obvious Design Is the Wrong One

Single-node rate limiting is easy: a token bucket in memory, refilled at a fixed rate. The difficulty is entirely in the distributed case, and the obvious design fails in an instructive way.

The obvious design is a shared counter in Redis, incremented by every gateway on every request. It is exactly correct, and it means every single request now has a synchronous network round trip to one machine before it can be served. You have added roughly 1 ms of latency to 100% of traffic, created a hard dependency on Redis for your entire edge, and built a hotspot that limits your total throughput to what one Redis key can sustain. You have spent a great deal to enforce a limit whose entire purpose is approximate.

The better design applies the same move as P2C. Each gateway holds a local token bucket sized to its fair share — with k gateways and a global limit of R, each gets R/k — and gateways reconcile with a shared store asynchronously, every few hundred milliseconds, to redistribute unused allowance. The common path touches no network. The limit is enforced approximately, with a bounded error proportional to the reconciliation interval.

The right question at this point is not “how do we make it exact?” but “what is the cost of being wrong by 5%?” For abuse prevention: nothing, the limit is a heuristic anyway. For a paid API tier: also nothing, because you will refund a disputed overage far more cheaply than you will operate a globally exact counter. For metering that bills the customer directly: now exactness matters — and the correct response is to move billing off the request path entirely and compute it from an event log, rather than to make the rate limiter strongly consistent.

FIXED WINDOW -- the 2x burst hiding at the boundary limit: 100 requests per minute |------ window 1 ------|------ window 2 ------| 10:00 10:01 10:02 100 reqs 100 reqs at 10:00:59 at 10:01:01 \ / \ / 200 requests in a 2-second span Both windows are individually within their limit. The limiter is working exactly as specified and the backend still sees 2x the intended peak. SLIDING WINDOW COUNTER -- the cheap fix, and the one to name in an interview: weight the previous window by how much of it still overlaps the current one. at 10:01:15, 75% of window 1 is still in scope, so: estimate = (100 x 0.75) + count_so_far_in_window_2 Two counters per key, no sorted set of timestamps, error under 1% on real traffic. A sliding window LOG is exact but stores every timestamp, which is what makes it too expensive to be the default.
The fixed-window boundary burst is the most common rate-limiting bug in production and it never shows up in testing, because it only appears when traffic happens to cluster near a window edge — which real traffic does, since clients synchronise on wall-clock minutes.
✎ Mini exercise 14

Your API enforces 1,000 requests/minute per customer across 20 gateway nodes, using local token buckets of 50 requests each with reconciliation every 500 ms. A customer complains that they are being throttled at roughly 300 requests/minute, well under their limit.

Work out: what is happening, and what you change.

Show the worked answer

The customer's traffic is not spread evenly across the 20 gateways. Local bucket sizing assumes each node sees 1/20th of that customer's requests, and that assumption is broken by essentially every real routing layer: connection reuse pins a client to a small number of gateways, DNS and anycast route them by geography, and a customer calling from one region reaches perhaps three or four gateways rather than twenty.

If they reach 6 gateways, they can spend 6 × 50 = 300 requests per reconciliation period, and the other 14 buckets sit full and unused. The observed 300/minute is the arithmetic working exactly as built. The rate limiter is not broken; the fair-share assumption underneath it is.

What to change, in order of preference. First, make reconciliation redistributive rather than merely reporting: a node that exhausts its bucket should be able to borrow unused allowance from the global pool, so idle buckets are not stranded. This alone fixes most of it. Second, shorten the reconciliation interval for keys observed to be hot — you do not need 500 ms precision for the 99% of customers nowhere near their limit, so spend the coordination budget only where it changes an outcome. Third, and best if your routing layer allows it, make the constraint local for real by consistently hashing each customer to a small subset of gateways, so the fair-share denominator matches reality instead of being assumed.

The transferable principle: when you divide a global budget into local shares, you have assumed a distribution — and an unstated distributional assumption is a bug waiting for traffic to find it. The same error appears in Chapter 5 as the even-partition assumption that hot keys violate, and in Chapter 9 as the fixed cache budget that a new key pattern silently reallocates.

Load Shedding, Retry Storms, and Why Systems Fail to Recover

Rate limiting protects you from a specific caller. Load shedding protects you from everyone at once, and it is the mechanism that decides whether an overload is a bad ten minutes or a four-hour outage.

The distinction that matters: a rate limiter answers “has this client had its share?” A load shedder answers “can I serve anything at all right now?” A system with perfect per-client rate limits can still collapse, because the sum of everyone's legitimate allowance can exceed what you can serve when a dependency slows down.

What makes overload genuinely dangerous is that it is metastable: it can sustain itself after its original cause is gone. The loop is worth memorising, because it is the shape of most large outages.

THE METASTABLE FAILURE LOOP a dependency slows down (or a cache tier restarts) ▼ request latency rises above the client timeout ▼ clients time out and RETRY ▼ offered load is now 2x or 3x the original ▼ latency rises further; more clients time out ▼ back to the top, now self-sustaining The cruel part: the server is doing MORE work than before, not less -- it is computing responses for requests whose clients gave up and left. That work is pure waste, and it is crowding out the requests that could still be served in time. Fixing the original dependency does NOT recover the system. The retry backlog keeps offered load above capacity indefinitely. This is why an outage often outlives its cause by hours, and why recovery usually requires SHEDDING load or draining traffic entirely -- letting the queue empty -- rather than waiting.
The defining property of a metastable failure is that the system has two stable states — healthy, and collapsed — and enough load pushes it across a threshold from which it will not return on its own. Capacity planning tells you where the threshold is; load shedding is what stops you crossing it.
⚠ Common misconception
“We use exponential backoff, so we are safe from retry storms.”

Exponential backoff without jitter synchronises your clients rather than spreading them. If 10,000 clients fail at the same instant — which is what a dependency outage does — they all wait 1 s, then all retry together; then all wait 2 s, and all retry together. You have converted a continuous overload into a series of sharp, perfectly aligned spikes, and each spike is large enough to re-trigger the failure. Randomised (jittered) backoff is not a refinement of the idea; it is the part that makes it work.

And even jittered backoff only controls timing, never volume. Under a sustained failure, every client is still eventually retrying and total offered load still exceeds capacity. The mechanism that bounds volume is a retry budget: a client may retry only if retries have been under some small fraction — 10% is the common choice — of its recent request volume. When the dependency is broadly failing, the budget is exhausted almost immediately and retries stop altogether, which is exactly correct. Retries exist to paper over independent, transient failures; when the failure is systemic there is nothing to paper over, and retrying only adds load to something already drowning.

The complete answer is all three together: jitter spreads timing, a retry budget caps volume, and a circuit breaker stops the calls entirely once failure is established. Naming only backoff is the most common incomplete answer to this question.

🧠 Checking your understanding — Load balancing & rate limiting

Answers supplied. These separate people who have configured a load balancer from people who understand what it is doing.
When is L4 load balancing genuinely the right choice over L7?
When you do not need to look inside the request, and increasingly when you cannot. L4 balances TCP connections without parsing anything, so it is dramatically cheaper, adds almost no latency, and can pass encrypted traffic straight through without terminating TLS. Choose it for raw throughput, for non-HTTP protocols, and when end-to-end encryption to the backend is a requirement. Choose L7 when routing depends on content — path-based routing, header-based canaries, per-endpoint rate limits — or when you want request-level retries, which L4 fundamentally cannot do because it has no idea where one request ends and the next begins on a reused connection. That last point is the one people miss: connection reuse means an L4 balancer's “least connections” is counting something only loosely related to load.
Should a rate limiter fail open or fail closed when its backing store is unavailable?
Almost always fail open, and the reasoning is about relative blast radius. Failing closed means a Redis outage becomes a total outage of your API — you have made an availability dependency out of a component whose entire job is protective. Failing open means that during a Redis outage you are briefly unprotected against abuse, which is a much smaller and much less likely harm than refusing all traffic. The exception is when the limit is enforcing something whose violation is irreversible: a financial transfer cap, or a limit protecting a downstream system that will corrupt rather than merely slow. The staff-level answer adds a third option: fail open into a conservative local limit, so you degrade from precise global limiting to approximate per-node limiting instead of degrading to none.
How do you shed load well, given you must reject someone?
Reject by priority and by cost, never uniformly. Uniform shedding rejects 10% of every user's requests, which breaks 100% of user journeys partway through — the worst possible outcome, because a half-completed checkout is worth less than nothing. Better: classify traffic (health checks and payments above browsing and analytics), shed the cheapest-to-reject and least valuable first, and shed at the edge where rejection is cheap rather than after the request has already consumed a database connection. Critically, reject fast: a 429 returned in 1 ms frees capacity, while a request that times out after 30 seconds consumed a connection slot for 30 seconds and helped no one. Rejecting early is a form of doing work.
Why can adding a retry make a system less available overall?
Because retries multiply load exactly when load is the problem. A service at 80% utilisation has 25% headroom; a client retry policy of three attempts turns a partial failure into 3× offered load, which is far past capacity, and the additional load causes the failures that trigger more retries. Retries are also frequently nested — the client retries, the gateway retries, the service retries its own dependency — and nesting multiplies rather than adds, so three layers of three attempts is 27× amplification against the bottom service. The rule that follows: retry at exactly one layer, the one closest to the user that can still make a meaningful decision, and pass failures through everywhere else.
What does a health check actually tell you, and how does it lie?
A shallow health check (“is the process listening?”) tells you almost nothing — a process can accept connections while every dependency behind it is dead. A deep check that verifies dependencies is more truthful but introduces a catastrophic failure mode: if the shared database becomes slow, every backend fails its deep check simultaneously, the load balancer removes all of them, and a degradation becomes a total outage. The standard defence is a minimum healthy threshold — if more than some fraction of the fleet is unhealthy, assume the checker is wrong rather than the fleet, and keep routing to everyone. This is Chapter 1's lesson applied to health: you cannot distinguish a broken backend from a broken observation of a backend, so refuse to take drastic action on evidence that says everything is broken at once.
Token bucket or leaky bucket — how do you actually choose?
Ask whether bursts are legitimate. A token bucket accumulates tokens while idle, so a client that has been quiet may spend a burst all at once — ideal for user-facing APIs, where a page load that fires 20 requests at once is normal behaviour and should not be punished. A leaky bucket drains at a fixed rate and permits no burst at all, which is what you want when the thing being protected has a hard physical throughput ceiling and genuinely cannot absorb a spike — a downstream partner's API, a mainframe, a physical device. In short: token bucket smooths the average and tolerates bursts; leaky bucket smooths the instantaneous rate and eliminates them. Most public APIs should be token buckets, and most integrations with someone else's fragile system should be leaky ones.
🎯 Which strategy real systems choose, and why
Stateless web tier
P2C at L7. Requests are independent and cheap to route, and the tail latency benefit is free. Global least-connections would be more accurate and would risk herding.
Long-lived WebSocket fleet
Least-connections, and it genuinely matters here: connections last hours, so a bad placement decision is not corrected by the next request the way it is for HTTP. Ch 11
Cache tier
Consistent hashing, not load balancing at all — the request must reach the node holding the key. Balance is sacrificed for locality, and hot keys are then handled separately. Ch 5
Public API gateway
Local token buckets with asynchronous reconciliation. Approximate global limits, no per-request coordination, and it fails open into a local limit.
Internal service mesh
Concurrency limits rather than rate limits. Bounding in-flight requests adapts automatically as backend speed changes, whereas a fixed requests-per-second limit is wrong the moment latency shifts.
Payments / irreversible actions
The one place to consider failing closed, plus idempotency keys so that a retry after an ambiguous timeout cannot double-charge. Ch 7
🌱 Takeaway — Load balancing & rate limiting

Both halves of this chapter are the same idea: a local, approximate decision beats a global, exact one.

  • Balance work, not request counts. Round robin has no feedback channel, so it feeds a struggling backend at full rate until it dies.
  • Power of two choices is the best value in the chapter. One extra probe takes tail load from log n/log log n to log log n, with no shared state and no herding.
  • Do not put a synchronous counter on every request. Local buckets plus redistributive reconciliation; then ask what a 5% error actually costs, and move billing off the request path if the honest answer is “too much”.
  • Fixed windows permit a 2× boundary burst. Sliding window counter: two counters, sub-1% error, no timestamp log.
  • Overload is metastable. It sustains itself after the cause is gone, because the server is busy computing answers for clients that already left. Recovery needs shedding, not patience.
  • Backoff needs jitter, a retry budget, and a circuit breaker. Backoff alone synchronises clients; only the budget bounds volume. And retry at exactly one layer, because nesting multiplies.

Chapter 11 takes the same pressure and removes the time coupling entirely: if the caller does not need an answer now, a queue lets you accept the work and serve it at your own pace.

Chapter 11
Message Queues & Streaming
Decoupling services with Kafka — and understanding exactly-once delivery.

Message queues are the connective tissue of large distributed systems. Instead of Service A calling Service B synchronously (tight coupling), A drops a message onto a queue, and B consumes it when ready (loose coupling). The queue absorbs traffic spikes, enables retry, and allows B to process at its own pace.

📖 Analogy

A restaurant kitchen uses a ticket system: waiters write orders on tickets and hang them on a rail. The kitchen cooks work through tickets at their own pace. If a rush of customers arrive, tickets pile up — but the kitchen doesn't crash. This is exactly what a message queue does for microservices.

Why Kafka Became the Standard

Traditional message queues (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ) delete messages after a consumer acknowledges them. Kafka is fundamentally different — it's a distributed log. Messages are stored durably on disk and consumers track their own position (offset). Messages stay for days or weeks.

This enables something powerful: replay. If a bug is found in your analytics consumer, you fix the bug and replay from last week's messages. No data lost. This is impossible with traditional queues.

Kafka Internals — How It Actually Works

Kafka topics are split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log on disk.

Why Kafka Is Fast

Kafka achieves millions of messages/sec per broker because:

  • Sequential I/O: Appending to a log file is sequential. HDDs do sequential reads at 100+ MB/s; random reads at 100 KB/s. Kafka exploits sequential access completely.
  • OS page cache: Linux aggressively caches recently read/written disk data in RAM. Kafka's sequential access pattern means nearly all reads come from page cache — effectively RAM speed.
  • Zero-copy: sendfile() syscall copies data directly from OS page cache to NIC buffer, bypassing user space. No unnecessary copies.
  • Batching: Producers batch messages before sending. Consumers fetch in batches. Amortizes network overhead.

Delivery Guarantees

GuaranteeHowRiskUse For
At-most-onceSend and forget. No retry.Data loss if broker downTelemetry where loss is OK
At-least-onceRetry on failure. Consumer must handle duplicates.Duplicate messagesMost applications. Consumer must be idempotent.
Exactly-onceIdempotent producer + transactional consumerHigher latency, complexityFinancial transactions, deduplication-critical
🔬 Google-Level Depth — Exactly-Once in Kafka

Producer side (idempotent producer): Each producer gets a PID. Each message has a sequence number. Broker deduplicates: if it sees a message with a sequence number it already committed, it drops it. Retries are safe.

Consumer side (transactional): Wrap read-process-write in a Kafka transaction. Atomically commit the output message AND the consumed offset. Either both happen or neither. If the consumer crashes mid-way, the transaction is aborted — message is reprocessed. But the output is atomic so no duplicate outputs.

The cost: Each transaction has overhead. Used for critical financial streams where duplicate payments are catastrophic. For most applications, at-least-once with idempotent consumers (check 'have I seen this message ID?') achieves effectively-exactly-once with less complexity.

📝 Interview Q&A

When would you choose Kafka over RabbitMQ?

Choose Kafka when: (1) You need message replay — consuming old messages again. (2) High throughput — millions of messages/sec. (3) Multiple consumers reading the same stream independently. (4) Event sourcing — the log IS the source of truth. (5) Stream processing with Kafka Streams/Flink.

Choose RabbitMQ when: (1) You need complex routing logic (topic/fanout/direct exchanges). (2) Message priority queues. (3) Individual message acknowledgment and requeuing. (4) Lower operational complexity (simpler than Kafka+ZooKeeper/KRaft).

The fundamental difference: Kafka is a distributed log (pull, retention, replay). RabbitMQ is a message broker (push, acknowledge, delete).

A consumer crashes after processing a message but before committing its offset. What happens?

The message is re-delivered. On restart, the consumer resumes from the last committed offset — which is before the crashed message. The message is processed again.

This means: Your consumer must be idempotent — processing the same message twice must produce the same result as processing it once. Design patterns: (1) Database insert with unique constraint on message_id — second insert fails harmlessly. (2) Check 'have I processed this message_id?' before processing. (3) Use Kafka transactions for atomic process + commit.

At-least-once delivery with idempotent processing is the standard pattern. Exactly-once transactions are reserved for cases where idempotency is impossible (e.g., sending an email — you can't check 'was this email already sent?' easily).
