Transcoding: 1 hour video -> 10 quality versions -> each 10x slower than realtime for 4K -> 1 hour -> 10 hours transcode time. Parallel transcode per quality. 500 hrs/min = 5,000 transcode-hours/min needed -> ~5,000 transcode VMs needed (1 hour video processed in 1 minute each).

[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Upload -> raw GCS -> Kafka event -> transcode fleet -> HLS segments in GCS -> CDN streams to viewers.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Resumable Upload: Large video files (10GB) cannot be sent in one HTTP request. Use chunked upload: split into 5MB chunks, upload each with offset. Server acknowledges each chunk. On failure: resume from last acknowledged chunk. Google Cloud Storage's XML API and TUS protocol implement this pattern.

Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (HLS): Transcoded video is split into 2-10 second segments (.ts files). A manifest file (.m3u8) lists all segments and their quality levels. The client player requests segments and monitors download speed. If downloading 720p segments is slow (bandwidth dropped), it switches to 480p manifest automatically. This gives smooth playback without buffering.

Transcoding pipeline: One Kafka event per upload. Transcoding worker pool: each worker fetches the raw video from GCS, transcodes one quality level (FFmpeg), uploads HLS segments to GCS, acknowledges Kafka. Multiple workers process different quality levels in parallel. Status tracked in PostgreSQL (video_id, status: transcoding/ready, progress %).

CDN strategy: HLS segments are immutable (content-addressed by segment hash). Cache-Control: max-age=31536000 (1 year). CDN naturally geo-distributes popular content. New videos: cold start -- first viewers get from GCS. After 100 views: cached at every CDN edge worldwide.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
TranscodingAsync Kafka pipeline (eventual availability)Sync (block upload until done)Sync transcode = wait 5-60 min for every upload. Terrible UX. Async = upload acknowledged immediately, video available in ~5 min. Acceptable.
Streaming formatHLS (HTTP Live Streaming)RTMP / WebRTCHLS works over standard CDN HTTP. RTMP requires special servers. WebRTC good for sub-second latency (live streaming) but overkill for pre-recorded video. HLS adaptive bitrate = optimal for variable bandwidth.
StorageGCS object storageHDFS / customGCS: 11-nine durability, petabyte scale, CDN integration, managed. HDFS: operational burden, no CDN, doesn't scale to exabytes easily.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Transcode worker crashes mid-job
Kafka offset not committed until job complete. Worker crash -> message re-delivered -> new worker picks up from beginning (idempotent: transcode is pure function, same input = same output). Partial segments discarded.
GCS regional outage
Multi-region GCS bucket (US + EU). If primary region down, read from secondary with minimal latency increase. Writes queued and replayed when primary recovers. CDN cache continues serving most traffic during outage.
CDN node failure
CDN routes around failed edge nodes automatically. Traffic shifts to next-nearest edge. Brief latency increase. Popular content likely cached on multiple edges.

Design a Distributed Job Scheduler (like AWS Lambda / Cron)

Difficulty: Medium-Hard  .  Target: 40 min
[list] 1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Schedule jobs: run at specific time (one-shot) or cron expression (recurring)
  • Each job has a handler (function/URL to call)
  • Exactly-once execution: a job must not run twice at the same scheduled time
  • At-least-once fallback: if execution fails, retry with backoff
  • Job status tracking: pending/running/succeeded/failed
  • 10M+ scheduled jobs, 100K jobs/sec at peak

Non-Functional:

  • Job fires within 1 second of scheduled time
  • No duplicate execution (critical)
  • Retry on failure (configurable: max retries, backoff)
  • HA: 99.99% -- scheduler failure must not cause missed jobs
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Jobs table (PostgreSQL -- ACID needed for scheduling locks) TABLE jobs { job_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(255), cron_expr VARCHAR(100), -- NULL for one-shot next_run_at TIMESTAMP, handler_url TEXT, payload JSONB, status ENUM(pending, running, succeeded, failed), retry_count INT DEFAULT 0, max_retries INT DEFAULT 3, last_run_at TIMESTAMP, locked_by VARCHAR(64), -- worker_id holding lock lock_expires TIMESTAMP -- fencing: lock expires if worker crashes } -- INDEX: (next_run_at, status) WHERE status = 'pending' -- This index allows efficient polling: 'give me pending jobs due now'
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Scheduler polls DB with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED -- atomic claim prevents double execution. Workers execute via Kafka.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

The Double Execution Problem -- Most Critical: Two scheduler instances both see a job due at T=1000. Both try to execute it. The job runs twice. For a payment job, this double-charges the customer.

Solution: SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE next_run_at <= NOW() AND status='pending' LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
This SQL atomically locks selected rows. A second scheduler running the same query will SKIP the already-locked rows and get different jobs. Completely prevents double-execution at the DB level. No application-level coordination needed.

Fencing against worker crashes: After claiming a job, set lock_expires = NOW() + 5 min. Worker must heartbeat every minute. If worker crashes, lock_expires passes -> background sweeper resets status to 'pending' -> job gets re-scheduled. Lock_expires is a fencing token: the crashed worker cannot complete the job after recovery (its lock has expired).

Scheduler high availability: Multiple scheduler instances. Only one is active (leader election via etcd/ZooKeeper/DB advisory lock). Follower schedulers are on hot standby. Leader failure -> follower takes over in <30s. With SELECT FOR UPDATE, even if two schedulers are briefly both active, no double execution.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
Job claimSELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKEDDistributed lock (Redis)DB-level locking eliminates network round-trip to external lock service. SKIP LOCKED allows concurrent schedulers without contention. Simpler -- no lock service dependency.
Exactly-onceDB lock + idempotent handler contractTransactionsFull exactly-once requires handler to be idempotent (we guarantee at-most-once delivery; handler must handle retries). Telling customers: 'your handler may run twice on failure -- make it idempotent' is standard practice.
DeliveryPull (DB poll every 1s)Push (DB triggers)DB triggers couple scheduler to DB internals. Poll is simple, predictable, scalable. 1-second poll granularity acceptable for most cron use cases. Sub-second scheduling needs a different architecture.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Scheduler leader crashes
Follower detects via etcd lease expiry (~15s). Takes over leadership. Jobs due during those 15s: lock_expires hasn't passed, so they're safe. After 15s: new leader picks up pending jobs. Max 15-second delay.
Worker crashes mid-execution
lock_expires passes -> sweeper resets job to pending -> re-executed. Handler MUST be idempotent (most are: send email with idempotency key, write to DB with upsert). Document this contract clearly.
DB (PostgreSQL) failure
Primary fails -> replica promoted (RDS Multi-AZ: ~30s). Schedulers lose DB connection, buffer job picks in memory (Kafka), retry DB connection. No jobs lost. Some delayed by up to ~1 min.

Design a Distributed Message Queue (Apache Kafka / Google Cloud PubSub)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  •  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements

Functional Requirements:

  • Producers publish messages to named topics with optional partition keys.
  • Consumers subscribe to topics as part of Consumer Groups and consume sequentially.
  • Strict FIFO ordering within a single partition; total order across partitions is non-goal.
  • Configurable message retention (time-based e.g., 7 days, or size-based) independent of consumption status.
  • High throughput and low latency pub/sub delivery with replayability.

Non-Functional Requirements:

  • Throughput: 1,000,000 messages/sec write, 5,000,000 messages/sec read (fan-out 5x).
  • Latency: Produce p99 < 10ms, End-to-end consume latency < 50ms.
  • Durability: Zero data loss (RPO = 0) with multi-replica sync replication.
  • High Availability: 99.99% uptime (SLA), automatic partition leader failover < 5s.

// 1. Produce Message (gRPC / TCP Streaming) rpc Produce(ProduceRequest) returns (ProduceResponse); message ProduceRequest { string topic = 1; int32 partition = 2; // -1 for hash(key) auto-routing bytes key = 3; bytes payload = 4; int32 acks = 5; // 0=no ack, 1=leader ack, -1(all)=ISR ack int64 producer_id = 6; // for idempotent deduplication int32 sequence_number = 7; } // 2. Fetch / Consume Messages (Long Polling Batch) rpc Fetch(FetchRequest) returns (FetchResponse); message FetchRequest { string consumer_group = 1; string topic = 2; int32 partition = 3; int64 fetch_offset = 4; int32 max_bytes = 5; // e.g. 1MB batch int32 max_wait_ms = 6; // long-poll timeout (e.g. 500ms) } // 3. Commit Offset rpc CommitOffset(CommitRequest) returns (CommitResponse); message CommitRequest { string consumer_group = 1; string topic = 2; int32 partition = 3; int64 committed_offset = 4; }
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Log Segment File Structure on Broker Disk -- File: /data/kafka/topics/{topic_name}-{partition_id}/{base_offset}.log -- Append-Only Binary Record Format: [Offset: 8B][Size: 4B][CRC: 4B][Magic: 1B][Attributes: 1B][Timestamp: 8B] [Key_Length: 4B][Key_Bytes][Value_Length: 4B][Payload_Bytes] -- Sparse Memory-Mapped Index: {base_offset}.index -- Every 4KB of log data, append entry (Relative Offset: 4B, Physical Byte Position: 4B) [Rel_Offset: 0 -> Pos: 0] [Rel_Offset: 120 -> Pos: 4096] [Rel_Offset: 245 -> Pos: 8192] -- Consumer Offset Tracking (__consumer_offsets internal compacted topic) KEY: (consumer_group_id, topic, partition_id) VALUE: (offset: int64, commit_timestamp: int64, metadata: string)
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Zero-copy pagecache pipeline: writes bypass JVM heap into OS pagecache; reads stream directly from pagecache to NIC using sendfile()
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

1. Why Kafka is blistering fast (The 4 Pillars of Performance):

  • Sequential I/O over Random Access: Disks (both HDD and NVMe) provide orders of magnitude higher throughput for sequential append operations vs random seeks. Kafka only appends to the active segment file.
  • PageCache Utilization: Kafka delegates caching to the Linux OS PageCache rather than maintaining an in-memory cache in the JVM heap. This avoids GC pauses, simplifies broker restarts (PageCache survives JVM restarts), and eliminates memory duplication.
  • Zero-Copy Data Transfer (sendfile): In standard architectures, reading from disk to network requires 4 context switches and 3 data copies (Disk -> OS PageCache -> JVM Heap -> Socket Buffer -> NIC Buffer). Kafka uses sendfile() syscall, transferring data directly from PageCache to NIC buffer (0 CPU copies, 2 context switches).
  • End-to-End Batching & Compression: Producers batch messages by partition and compress them (Zstandard/Snappy). Brokers store compressed batches untouched, and consumers decompress them. Network and disk bandwidth are reduced by 4x-10x.

2. In-Sync Replicas (ISR) and High Watermark (HW):

Each partition has 1 Leader and N Follower replicas. Followers continuously fetch messages from the leader. If a follower falls behind by more than replica.lag.time.max.ms (default 30s), it is dropped from the ISR. The High Watermark (HW) is the highest offset replicated to ALL nodes in the ISR. Consumers can ONLY read messages up to the HW. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, no message is lost if a leader crashes.

3. Idempotent & Transactional Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS):

Each producer is assigned a 64-bit ProducerId (PID) by the broker coordinator. For every partition, the producer tracks a monotonically increasing SequenceNumber. The broker rejects any duplicate sequence number. For multi-partition atomic writes (Read-Process-Write cycle), a Two-Phase Commit Transaction Coordinator maintains a __transaction_state log and writes COMMIT/ABORT markers into topic partitions.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Storage EngineAppend-Only Segmented LogB-Tree / Embedded DB (RocksDB)Log gives O(1) disk writes, sequential reads, and instant zero-copy transfer. B-Trees incur random writes, write amplification, and complex locking.
Replication ConsensusISR with Quorum Controller (KRaft)Paxos / Raft per partitionISR allows dynamic quorum based on live replica speed, achieving maximum write throughput. KRaft manages cluster metadata with a single Raft quorum instead of ZooKeeper.
Consumption ModelPull (Long-Polling by Consumers)Push (Broker pushes to clients)Pull lets consumers pace themselves according to their processing capacity (eliminating consumer overload) and simplifies batch fetching and replay.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Leader Broker Crashes
KRaft controller detects heartbeat failure in <3s. Elects new leader from the ISR pool. No committed data is lost because ISR nodes are byte-for-byte in sync up to HW.
Slow / Stalled Follower
Controller evicts the lagging node from ISR so it does not block produce requests when acks=all. Once caught up, it rejoins the ISR.
Consumer Crashes during processing
Consumer group coordinator detects missed heartbeat (session.timeout.ms). Triggers Consumer Group Rebalance, reassigning crashed consumer's partitions to remaining workers from last committed offset.
Split Brain in Controller Quorum
KRaft uses Raft majority quorum (e.g. 3 of 5 nodes). A network partition cannot elect an illegitimate leader in the minority partition.

Initiate Resumable Chunked Upload POST /api/v1/files/upload/init Header: Authorization: Bearer {token}, Idempotency-Key: {uuid} Body: { "filename": "annual_report.pdf", "folder_id": "f_98234", "total_bytes": 41943040, "chunk_hashes": ["sha256_chunk1", "sha256_chunk2", ...] } Response: 200 OK { "upload_id": "upl_8723", "missing_chunk_hashes": ["sha256_chunk2", "sha256_chunk5"], // Server deduplicates existing chunks! "presigned_s3_urls": { "sha256_chunk2": "https://s3.../chunk2", ... } } // 2. Commit File Version POST /api/v1/files/upload/commit Body: { "upload_id": "upl_8723", "file_id": "fil_1029", "version": 4, "chunk_hashes": ["sha256_chunk1", "sha256_chunk2", "sha256_chunk3"] } // 3. Real-Time Sync Event Stream (WebSocket / HTTP Long-Polling) GET /api/v1/sync/events?cursor={last_sync_seq_no}
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Metadata DB (CockroachDB / Spanner for global ACID consistency) TABLE files { file_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, workspace_id UUID, parent_folder_id UUID, name VARCHAR(255), latest_version INT, is_deleted BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE, created_at TIMESTAMP, updated_at TIMESTAMP } TABLE file_versions { file_id UUID, version_number INT, total_size BIGINT, checksum_sha256 CHAR(64), created_by UUID, created_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (file_id, version_number) } TABLE file_chunks { file_id UUID, version_number INT, chunk_index INT, chunk_hash CHAR(64) REFERENCES chunks(chunk_hash), PRIMARY KEY (file_id, version_number, chunk_index) } TABLE chunks { chunk_hash CHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY, byte_size INT, storage_path VARCHAR(512), -- S3 / GCS object key ref_count BIGINT -- GC: deleted when ref_count == 0 }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Content-defined chunking (Rabin Fingerprint) splits files into 4MB deduplicated blobs stored in S3; Spanner maintains atomic metadata; WebSockets notify sync clients
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

1. Content-Defined Chunking vs Fixed-Size Chunking:

If you split files by fixed 4MB offsets, inserting 1 byte at the start of a 100MB file shifts all subsequent offsets, changing the SHA-256 hash of every single chunk (0% deduplication). Rabin Fingerprinting / FastCDC calculates a rolling polynomial checksum over a sliding window. When the checksum's lowest 13 bits equal a constant (e.g. hash & 0x1FFF == 0), a chunk boundary is set. Inserting data only changes 1 or 2 chunks surrounding the insertion; all remaining chunks retain identical hashes and are deduplicated.

2. Conflict Resolution (Two users edit simultaneously offline):

Google Drive uses Optimistic Concurrency Control with version numbers. When Client A commits version 2 of file_1, it succeeds. When Client B later attempts to commit version 2 of file_1, the DB detects a version mismatch (expected v1, currently v2). The server rejects Client B's commit and creates a branch: annual_report (Client B's conflicted copy 2026-09-07).pdf. For collaborative text docs (Google Docs), Operational Transformation (OT) or CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) resolve character-level conflicts in real time.

3. Garbage Collection for Chunks:

When files/versions are permanently deleted, chunks cannot be immediately removed from S3 because other files or users might share the same content-addressed hash. Each chunk row maintains a ref_count in the DB. When a version is purged, decrement ref_count. A daily MapReduce / Spark batch sweeper queries chunks with ref_count == 0 and deletes the underlying S3 objects.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Chunk SplittingClient-side Rabin ChunkingServer-side ChunkingClient-side saves huge upload bandwidth (never uploads chunks already in S3) and offloads CPU hashing from server infrastructure.
Metadata StoreSpanner / CockroachDB (NewSQL)Cassandra / DynamoDB (NoSQL)File tree operations (renaming a folder, moving 10,000 files) require atomic multi-row ACID transactions. NoSQL eventual consistency causes phantom or orphaned files.
Sync ProtocolDelta Sync with WebSocket notifyPeriodic Client PollingWebSockets deliver sub-second sync latency to all connected devices without hammering servers with millions of empty poll requests.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Upload Aborted Midway (Network drop)
Chunk uploads are idempotent. Client queries /upload/status with upload_id, receives list of already-persisted chunks, and resumes only the remaining chunks without re-uploading.
S3 / Cloud Storage Outage
Blob storage is multi-region replicated (e.g. S3 Cross-Region Replication). Read requests failover to secondary region CDN endpoint.
Metadata DB Primary Failure
Spanner / CockroachDB uses Multi-Paxos / Raft per range. Automatic leader election completes in <2s with zero data loss.
Zombie / Corrupt Chunks
Every downloaded chunk is verified against its expected SHA-256 hash by the client. If corrupted, client requests chunk from alternate replica.

Search Nearby Drivers GET /api/v1/drivers/nearby?lat=37.7749&lng=-122.4194&radius_m=3000&ride_type=UBER_X Response: 200 OK { "drivers": [ {"driver_id": "d_101", "lat": 37.7750, "lng": -122.4180, "eta_sec": 180, "bearing": 45.0}, ... ] } // 3. Request Ride (Idempotent Dispatch) POST /api/v1/trips/request Header: Idempotency-Key: {uuid} Body: { "rider_id": "r_901", "pickup_lat": 37.7749, "pickup_lng": -122.4194, "dropoff_lat": 37.7891, "dropoff_lng": -122.4014, "ride_type": "UBER_X", "fare_quote_id": "fq_7723" }
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Ephemeral Real-Time Geospatial Index (In-Memory Redis / Uber Ringpop H3) -- Redis Geospatial (GEOADD / GEORADIUS) or H3 Hexagonal Cell Sets: KEY: geo:h3:{h3_cell_index} -- e.g. geo:h3:8828308281fffff VALUE: SET of {driver_id} KEY: driver:{driver_id}:state VALUE: HASH { "lat": 37.7749, "lng": -122.4194, "status": "AVAILABLE", "h3_index": "8828308281fffff", "last_ping": 1725682910 } -- Trip State DB (CockroachDB / Cassandra for High Scale + ACID) TABLE trips { trip_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, rider_id UUID, driver_id UUID, status ENUM(requested, matched, arrived, in_progress, completed, canceled), pickup_lat DOUBLE, pickup_lng DOUBLE, dropoff_lat DOUBLE, dropoff_lng DOUBLE, fare_cents INT, created_at TIMESTAMP, updated_at TIMESTAMP }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Location ingestion is buffered via Kafka into H3 in-memory spatial shards; Dispatch Engine computes 1-ring neighbors and queries OSRM routing engine for precise traffic ETA
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

1. Spatial Indexing: Geohash vs Google S2 vs Uber H3:

  • Geohash (Rectangles): Encodes lat/lng into a base32 string (Z-order curve). Neighbor search has edge distortion at poles and cell boundaries vary drastically by latitude.
  • Google S2 (Spherical Hilbert Curve): Projects Earth onto 6 cube faces subdivided with a Hilbert curve. Great 1D index representation, but square cells have different distances to edge vs corner neighbors (factor of √2).
  • Uber H3 (Hexagonal Grid - Chosen): Subdivides the sphere into regular hexagons. Hexagons have the invariant that all 6 neighboring cells are equidistant from the center. This makes radius expansion (k-ring search: Ring 1 = 6 cells, Ring 2 = 12 cells) mathematically pure with zero corner distortion.

2. The Driver Matching Algorithm (DISCO):

Matching cannot just pick the nearest driver by Euclidean distance (they might be across a river or on a one-way highway).

  1. Lookup Rider's H3 cell (e.g. Resolution 8, ~460m).
  2. Fetch all AVAILABLE drivers in Rider's cell + k-ring(1) + k-ring(2) (total 1 + 6 + 12 = 19 hexagons).
  3. Batch call the Routing Engine (OSRM / Contraction Hierarchies) to calculate real street driving ETA considering traffic.
  4. Rank candidate drivers by ETA, driver acceptance rating, and supply-demand balance.
  5. Send dispatch offer to Top 1 driver with a 15-second TTL timer in Redis. If rejected/timed out, cascade to candidate #2.

3. Preventing Double Booking under Concurrency:

When two riders request a ride simultaneously in the same street corner, both may match with Driver D. To avoid double booking: The Dispatch Service executes a conditional atomic update on the driver's state in Redis/DB: UPDATE drivers SET status = 'DISPATCHED', active_trip_id = {trip_id} WHERE driver_id = {d_id} AND status = 'AVAILABLE'. If 0 rows updated, driver was already claimed; engine immediately selects next candidate.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Spatial GridUber H3 Hexagonal GridQuadtree / GeohashHexagons guarantee uniform neighbor distance in all 6 directions, drastically simplifying k-ring spatial smoothing and surge pricing calculations.
Location StorageIn-Memory Redis + TTL (Ephemeral)Persistent RDBMS / Disk DBDriver location pings are only relevant for ~30 seconds. Persisting 1.25M writes/sec to disk is wasteful. History is downsampled and written to cold analytics via Kafka.
Matching ArchitectureCentralized Dispatch (Batch Mini-Auction)Greedy First-Come-First-ServeBatching ride requests every 2-3 seconds achieves global optimization (minimizing total wait time for all riders) rather than greedily assigning the closest car to the first request.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Driver Loses Internet Mid-Trip
Driver app buffers GPS points in local SQLite. Upon reconnection, app uploads buffered breadcrumbs to reconcile route and compute accurate fare.
Dispatch Service Node Crashes during 15s offer
Driver offer is backed by Redis TTL key with an expiring lease. If dispatch node dies, heartbeat supervisor detects pending trip and re-dispatches to another driver.
Surge Traffic Spike (New Year's Eve 10x Load)
Rate limit nearby driver map refreshes from 4s to 8s per rider; drop unneeded background location telemetry while preserving dispatch pipeline.
Redis H3 Shard Failure
Redis Sentinel / Cluster promotes replica in <1s. Lost ephemeral driver pings are replenished within 4 seconds as drivers broadcast.

Design a Distributed Web Crawler & Search Indexer (Googlebot Architecture)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  •  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements

Functional Requirements:

  • Given a list of seed URLs, crawl billions of web pages across the public Internet.
  • Extract text content and outgoing hyperlinks to discover new URLs recursively.
  • Respect robots.txt rules and adhere to domain-level politeness (max 1 req/sec per host).
  • Deduplicate crawled content (avoid re-crawling identical or mirrored pages).
  • Store raw HTML / clean text in Document Store and update the Inverted Index for search.

Non-Functional Requirements:

  • Scale: Crawl 10 Billion pages per month (approx. 4,000 pages/sec continuous).
  • Storage: 10B pages × 100 KB avg clean text = 1 Petabyte storage per crawl cycle.
  • Freshness: Re-crawl dynamic sites (news) every few hours; static pages monthly.
  • Fault Tolerance: System must run 24/7 without deadlocks, handling spider traps and crashing hosts.
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
