[plug] 3. API Design
// URL Frontier Internal RPC Protocol (gRPC) rpc FetchUrlsToCrawl(FetchBatchRequest) returns (FetchBatchResponse); message FetchBatchRequest { string crawler_worker_id = 1; int32 max_urls = 2; // e.g. 500 URLs } message FetchBatchResponse { repeated CrawlTask tasks = 1; } message CrawlTask { string url = 1; string domain = 2; int32 crawl_delay_sec = 3; // parsed from robots.txt int32 depth = 4; } // Inverted Index Search RPC rpc SearchIndex(SearchQuery) returns (SearchResponse); message SearchQuery { string query_text = 1; // "distributed consensus raft" int32 limit = 2; int32 offset = 3; }
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- URL Frontier State (Distributed Bigtable / Cassandra) TABLE url_frontier { url_hash CHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY, -- SHA-256(canonical_url) url TEXT, domain_hash CHAR(32), status ENUM(discovered, queued, fetching, crawled, error), priority_score FLOAT, -- PageRank + Domain Authority last_crawled_at TIMESTAMP, etag VARCHAR(128), content_simhash BIGINT -- 64-bit SimHash for near-duplicate detection } -- Inverted Index (Distributed Sharded Posting Lists - MapReduce / Lucene) TABLE inverted_index { term VARCHAR(128) PRIMARY KEY, -- e.g. "raft" posting_list BLOB -- Compressed list of (doc_id, term_frequency, [positions]) } -- Example Posting List: -- "raft" -> [Doc#12: TF=5, Pos=[12,45,89]], [Doc#99: TF=2, Pos=[3,120]]
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
URL Frontier uses 2-tier Priority & Politeness Queues; Bloom Filters discard already-seen URLs; Parser indexes text and loops discovered URLs back into Frontier
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

1. The Mercator URL Frontier Architecture (Politeness + Priority):

To avoid hitting a single website (e.g. wikipedia.org) with 1,000 req/sec and causing a Denial of Service, the URL Frontier separates prioritization from politeness:

  • Priority Queues (F-Queues): Prioritizes URLs based on PageRank, domain authority, and freshness needs. High priority URLs are dequeued first into an intermediate router.
  • Politeness Queues (B-Queues): Each B-Queue contains URLs exclusively from a SINGLE host domain (e.g. Host #42 = nytimes.com). A scheduler maintains a min-heap of (next_allowed_fetch_time, B_queue_id). It only pops a queue if now() >= next_allowed_fetch_time (enforcing 1 req/sec per host), completely preventing DoS.

2. URL & Content Deduplication:

  • URL Dedup: A cluster Bloom Filter (stored in Redis or RAM) with 200B URLs at 1% false positive rate requires only ~240 GB RAM. If Bloom filter says 'Not Found', URL is 100% new. If 'Found', check Bigtable.
  • Near-Duplicate Content Detection (SimHash): 30% of web pages are duplicates or scrapers. Standard MD5/SHA256 changes completely on 1 character diff. SimHash projects 64-bit token hashes into a single 64-bit vector. Near-duplicate pages have a Hamming distance ≤ 3 (differ by at most 3 bits out of 64), which can be queried in O(1) time using a 4-table pigeonhole index.

3. Spider Traps & Infinite Dynamic Loops:

Websites with infinite calendar loops (/calendar?year=2027&month=13...) or session IDs in URLs trap crawlers. Defenses include: Max URL length limit (e.g. 512 chars), max path depth ≤ 8, URL pattern frequency monitoring per domain, and anomaly detection if a single domain yields > 50,000 URLs without new unique SimHash content.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
URL Seen TestBloom Filter + BigtableRDBMS Unique IndexBloom Filter answers 'seen' checks in 5 nanoseconds from memory, saving 4,000 expensive disk round-trips per second.
Near-Duplicate64-bit SimHash (Cosine distance)MinHash / Jaccard similaritySimHash produces a compact 8-byte fingerprint per document and enables bitwise Hamming distance comparisons with zero decompression.
Crawler StorageSSTable / Bigtable Sparse ColumnRelational DB / PostgresBigtable handles massive append throughput, automatic tablet sharding across petabytes, and compresses sparse web documents efficiently.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Fetcher Worker Freezes (Slow Server Response)
Fetchers use non-blocking asynchronous I/O (epoll/libuv) with hard 5-second socket read timeouts and 2MB response size caps.
DNS Resolution Bottleneck
Local custom caching DNS server with pre-fetching; eliminates 100ms DNS query delay per crawled page.
Frontier Master Node Failure
Frontier queue state is checkpointed to RocksDB / distributed log (Kafka). Standby master restores queue pointers in <5s.
Malicious Spider Trap / Zip Bomb
Decompression stream reader capped at 10MB; immediately aborts and blacklists the URL pattern if exceeded.

Design a Metrics & Logging Pipeline (Observability at Fleet Scale)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Ingest from 100,000 hosts emitting two different kinds of telemetry: metrics (numeric time series) and logs (semi-structured events)
  • Data queryable within 60 seconds of being emitted
  • Serve three consumers: dashboards (range queries), alerting (continuous evaluation), ad-hoc log search (forensics)
  • Tiered retention: metrics 13 months downsampled, raw logs 30 days

Non-Functional:

  • Ingest availability must exceed query availability — you can tolerate not being able to look, never losing the data you will need to look at
  • Must degrade under load rather than collapse, and must never become the cause of an incident
  • Cost-bounded: at this volume, storage cost is the design constraint
💡 The framing move that separates L6 from L5 here

Say this in the first three minutes: metrics and logs are two different systems and building them as one is the classic mistake. Metrics are numeric, aggregatable, and bounded by cardinality — you can pre-compute almost everything. Logs are unbounded, not aggregatable, and read rarely but urgently. They have opposite cost curves, so they get different storage engines behind a shared ingest path.

[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation

Assumptions: 100K hosts; 1,000 active metric series per host at 10s resolution; 100 log lines/sec per host at 300 bytes.

100M
active metric series
10M/s
metric datapoints
10M/s
log lines
3 GB/s
raw log bytes
~14 MB/s
compressed metrics
260 TB
raw logs/day

The number that decides the architecture: a metric datapoint compresses to roughly 1.4 bytes using delta-of-delta timestamps plus XOR-encoded floats (the Gorilla scheme), against 16 bytes uncompressed. So 10M datapoints/sec is only ~14 MB/s — about 1.2 TB/day. Logs at 10:1 gzip are ~26 TB/day.

Logs are ~20× the cost of metrics for a fraction of the query volume. That ratio is the entire justification for treating them differently, and it is the number to lead with when someone asks why you did not just use one system.

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /v1/ingest/metrics // protobuf, batched, gzip Body: { series: [{ name, labels{}, points:[{t, v}] }] } Response: 204, or 429 + Retry-After when shedding Note: fire-and-forget from the agent; NO synchronous ack path POST /v1/ingest/logs Body: { stream_labels{}, entries:[{t, line}] } Response: 204 | 429 GET /v1/query_range?q=&start=&end=&step= Response: { series:[{ labels{}, values:[[t,v]] }] } Errors: 422 series_limit_exceeded // reject, never OOM GET /v1/logs/search?selector=&filter=&start=&end=&limit= Response: streaming NDJSON, bounded by scan-bytes budget
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- METRICS: the label set IS the identity. Hash it once, store the mapping. TABLE series_index { series_id UINT64 PRIMARY KEY, -- hash(name + sorted labels) metric_name VARCHAR, labels MAP<str,str>, first_seen TIMESTAMP, last_seen TIMESTAMP -- drives churn detection + expiry } -- inverted index: label_name=label_value -> roaring bitmap of series_id BLOCK tsdb_block { -- immutable, 2h of data, columnar series_id, t0, delta_of_delta_ts[], xor_encoded_vals[] } -- ~1.4 bytes/point. Blocks compact 2h -> 1d -> 1w with rollups attached. -- LOGS: index the LABELS only, never the message body. TABLE log_chunk_index { stream_id UINT64, -- hash(stream_labels) t_start TIMESTAMP, t_end TIMESTAMP, object_key TEXT -- gzip chunk in object storage } -- Query = narrow by labels to a few chunks, then brute-force grep them.
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
100,000 hosts -- each runs a local AGENT (batches 10s, disk-buffers on failure) | v REGIONAL COLLECTORS stateless, terminate TLS, authenticate, validate, REJECT high-cardinality label sets at the door | v DURABLE LOG (Kafka) partitioned by series_id / stream_id | this is the shock absorber -- it decouples a | producer spike from consumer capacity +---------------------------+ v v METRICS CONSUMER LOG CONSUMER in-memory head block batch into 5-min gzip chunks WAL for crash recovery write chunk -> object store flush 2h block -> object write (stream_id, t_range, key) -> index | | v v TSDB QUERY LOG QUERY head (hot, RAM) + blocks label selector narrows to N chunks, downsampled rollups parallel scan with a bytes budget
The durable log in the middle is the whole design. Everything upstream of it is optimised for never dropping data; everything downstream can be restarted, rebuilt, or temporarily out of capacity without loss.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Cardinality is the failure mode — name it before you are asked. A metric series is identified by its full label set, so every distinct combination is a separate series with its own in-memory index entry and compression state. Adding one label with unbounded values — user_id, request_id, a raw URL with query parameters — turns one series into millions. The database does not slow down gracefully; the ingester's memory-resident index grows without bound and the process is OOM-killed. This is the single most common way a metrics system dies, and it is always caused by a well-meaning application change, never by traffic growth.

Defences, in order of effectiveness: reject at the collector with a per-tenant series budget so the blast radius is one team; alert on series churn (new series per minute) rather than absolute count, because churn is the leading indicator; and offer the escape hatch — if you need per-user granularity, that is a log or an exemplar, not a metric.

Why Gorilla compression matters so much. Timestamps in a scrape arrive at almost exactly fixed intervals, so the delta between consecutive deltas is nearly always zero and encodes in one bit. Values usually change slowly, so XOR-ing consecutive float64s leaves mostly leading zeros. Together this gives ~1.4 bytes/point — a 12× reduction that is what makes the entire recent window fit in RAM. A metrics system whose hot window is in memory answers dashboard queries in milliseconds; one that goes to disk cannot.

The log indexing decision. A full inverted index over log content (Elasticsearch-style) makes arbitrary text search fast and costs roughly as much as the raw data again in index size, plus heavy write-time CPU. Indexing labels only and brute-force scanning the matching chunks (Loki-style) makes ingest cheap and drops storage cost by an order of magnitude, at the price of slower unselective searches. Choose label-only indexing here: log search is rare, is nearly always already scoped by service and time, and the cost difference at 26 TB/day dominates the latency difference.

Rollups. Nobody queries 10-second resolution from six months ago; the dashboard would have more points than pixels. Compact blocks into 5-minute and 1-hour rollups carrying min/max/sum/count, and let the query layer pick resolution from the time range. This is what makes 13-month retention affordable, and it is a lossy decision you should state out loud.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Metrics vs logsTwo storage engines, one ingest pathOne unified storeOpposite cost curves. Logs are ~20x the bytes for a fraction of the queries. A unified store prices metrics like logs and makes 13-month retention unaffordable.
Ingest transportPush, via a durable logPull / scrapePull is simpler and gives free liveness detection, but cannot cross NAT or reach short-lived jobs. The durable log is non-negotiable regardless: it absorbs spikes that would otherwise reach the storage tier.
Log indexLabels only + brute scanFull inverted index~10x cheaper ingest and storage. Searches are almost always already narrowed by service and time window, so the unselective-query penalty is rarely paid.
Under overloadShed at the collector, 429Buffer indefinitelyUnbounded buffering converts an observability degradation into an observability outage, precisely when you need it. Shed low-priority tenants first and keep alerting metrics flowing.
Query safetyReject over series/byte budgetBest-effort executionOne unbounded query must not be able to OOM the node serving everyone's alerts. A fast 422 is a better answer than a slow death.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Kafka unavailable
Agents buffer to local disk with a bounded ring (e.g. 1 GB / 15 min) and resume on recovery. Beyond the bound they drop oldest first, because in an incident the newest telemetry is the telemetry you need. Collectors return 429 so agents back off with jitter.
Metrics ingester crashes
The in-memory head block is backed by a write-ahead log on local disk; on restart it replays the WAL to reconstruct the head. Kafka consumer offsets are committed only after the WAL write, so recovery is at-least-once. Duplicate datapoints are idempotent — same series, same timestamp, same value overwrites harmlessly.
Cardinality bomb from one team
Per-tenant series budget enforced at the collector: series beyond the budget are rejected with a named error and an alert to the owning team. Blast radius is one tenant instead of the cluster. This is the single most important safeguard in the design.
Object storage degraded
Recent data is still served from the in-memory head and local blocks, so dashboards and alerting for the last few hours keep working — which is the window that matters during an incident. Historical queries fail fast with a clear error rather than hanging.
The observability system causes an incident
Agents are hard-capped on CPU and memory via cgroups and drop telemetry rather than compete with the application they observe. Ingest endpoints are on separate capacity from query, so a dashboard stampede during an outage cannot block ingestion. This inversion — monitoring taking down production — is common enough that you should raise it unprompted.

Design a Distributed Cache (like Memcached / Redis Cluster)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
[list] 1. Requirements

Functional:

  • GET, SET with TTL, DELETE, atomic INCR
  • 10 TB working set across the cluster; values from 100 B to 1 MB
  • Elastic: add and remove nodes without a full cache flush

Non-Functional:

  • 10M QPS aggregate, p99 under 1 ms at the cache (excluding network to caller)
  • Cache loss is survivable — this is not a database — but a mass simultaneous loss must not take the origin down
  • No strong consistency requirement; the cache may serve a stale value
💡 Scope the problem before designing it

The clarifying question that earns the most here: “is this a cache or a low-latency store?” If the answer is cache, you may lose data freely and the design is about locality and eviction. If the answer is store, you need replication and durability and you are designing something two orders of magnitude more expensive. Most candidates assume the first and never say so; saying it out loud is the staff signal.

[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation

Assumptions: 10 TB working set, average value 1 KB, 10M QPS at 95:5 read:write.

~10B
keys resident
~64 GB
usable RAM/node
~200
nodes (with headroom)
50K
QPS per node avg
~10 GB/s
aggregate value bytes
~1.4 TB
overhead at 120B/key

The overhead nobody estimates: every entry carries key bytes, a hash-table slot, LRU pointers, TTL and flags — roughly 50–120 bytes before your value. With 1 KB values that is ~10% waste; with 100-byte values it is more than half your RAM. If the workload is small values, the correct answer is to change the workload — pack many logical entries into one cache entry — not to buy more nodes.

Sanity check the network, not just the memory: 10M QPS × 1 KB ≈ 10 GB/s aggregate, or ~50 MB/s per node. Comfortable. But a single hot key at 1M QPS × 1 KB is 1 GB/s to one node — an 8 Gbps NIC saturated by one key. Hot keys are a bandwidth problem before they are a CPU problem.

[plug] 3. API Design
// Binary protocol over pooled, pipelined TCP. No HTTP -- header // parsing alone would dominate a sub-millisecond budget. GET key -> value, cas_token | MISS MGET key[] -> values[] // one RTT for N keys, same node SET key value ttl flags -> STORED CAS key value cas_token -> STORED | EXISTS // compare-and-swap: the ONLY concurrency primitive here, // and what makes read-modify-write safe without a lock DELETE key -> DELETED | NOT_FOUND INCR key delta -> new_value // server-side, atomic // Client-side: routing table + consistent hash ring, refreshed // from a config service. The client picks the node -- no proxy hop.
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Per node: slab allocator, NOT malloc. Fixed-size classes in a -- growth factor (1.25x): 96B, 120B, 152B, 192B ... 1MB STRUCT item { next, prev PTR -- LRU list linkage h_next PTR -- hash chain expiry UINT32 -- lazy: checked on read, not swept nbytes, flags UINT32 cas_id UINT64 -- bumped on every mutation key[], value[] BYTES } -- Rounding to a slab class wastes up to 20% per item. That is the -- price of never fragmenting -- a cache that fragments dies slowly -- over weeks, which is far worse than a fixed 20% tax. -- Ring: 200 physical nodes x ~200 virtual nodes = 40,000 points. -- Virtual nodes are what make removal move 1/N of keys, not half.
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
APPLICATION + smart client library | | 1. hash(key) -> position on the ring | 2. walk clockwise to the owning virtual node | 3. connect DIRECTLY -- no proxy, no extra hop v CONSISTENT HASH RING 200 nodes x 200 vnodes = 40,000 points | +-------------+-------------+-------------+ v v v v node 1 node 2 node 3 ... node 200 slab alloc slab alloc slab alloc hash table hash table hash table LRU chains LRU chains LRU chains CONFIG SERVICE (small, strongly consistent -- etcd/Zookeeper) holds the authoritative ring; clients poll and cache it. Only membership needs consensus. Ch 6's expensive machinery is bought for a few KB of topology, never for the 10M QPS data path. HOT KEY PATH: keys above a QPS threshold are promoted to a client-local L1 (a few ms TTL) and replicated to R nodes, with the client picking one at random.
The single most important structural decision is that the data path touches no coordinator. Consensus is confined to membership, which changes a few times a week; the 10M QPS path is a hash computation and one round trip.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Why consistent hashing, in one number. With plain hash(key) mod N, changing N from 200 to 201 remaps roughly 99.5% of keys — a total cache flush and an instant origin stampede. Consistent hashing remaps only the keys owned by the departing node, about 1/N ≈ 0.5%. Virtual nodes are what make that share even: with one point per node, hash positions cluster and a removal dumps its whole range onto a single neighbour, which then falls over. Roughly 200 virtual nodes per physical node brings load variance under about 5%.

The hot key problem, which is where this interview actually goes. Consistent hashing distributes keys evenly; it cannot distribute traffic evenly, because traffic is Zipfian. One celebrity key can take 1M QPS to a single node while the other 199 idle. Three defences, and they compose:

  • Client-side L1 with a very short TTL (5–50 ms). A hot key is by definition read constantly, so even a 10 ms TTL collapses 1M QPS into ~100 QPS per client. This is the highest-leverage fix and it costs almost nothing, because the staleness it introduces is bounded by a number you choose.
  • Replicate hot keys to R nodes under salted names (key#1 … key#R), with clients picking one at random. Divides load by R at the cost of R× the memory for those keys and R invalidations per write.
  • Detect, do not guess. Track approximate per-key request rates with a count-min sketch on each node — sublinear memory, tolerable error — and promote keys past a threshold automatically. Static hot-key lists are always stale by the time they matter.

Eviction at scale. Strict LRU needs a lock on the list head for every read, which is a global mutex on your hottest path and will not sustain 50K QPS per node. Real implementations approximate: bump an item's position only if it has not been bumped in the last ~60 seconds, or use a CLOCK/second-chance bit. You give up exact recency ordering — which was only ever a heuristic — and you get a lock-free read path. Approximating the approximation is free.

Expiry is lazy, not swept. Actively scanning 10 billion keys for expired entries would burn CPU proportional to cache size rather than to traffic. Instead, check the TTL on read and let LRU reclaim the rest. The consequence to state: expired-but-unread entries still occupy memory, so your usable capacity is always somewhat below your nominal capacity.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
RoutingSmart client, direct connectProxy tierA proxy adds a network hop -- often 0.3-0.5 ms against a sub-1 ms budget -- plus a tier to scale and fail. A proxy wins only when you cannot control the clients or need many languages; then pay the hop deliberately.
PartitioningConsistent hashing + vnodeshash mod Nmod N remaps ~99.5% of keys when one node joins. That is a full flush and a guaranteed origin stampede at exactly the wrong moment.
ReplicationNone, except hot keysReplicate everythingDoubles cost to protect data that is by definition reconstructible. Spend that memory on a larger working set instead -- a bigger cache raises the hit rate, which is worth more than surviving one node loss.
EvictionApproximate LRUStrict LRUStrict LRU requires a lock on the list head per read. The recency ordering it buys was already a heuristic; the lock contention is real.
ConsistencyDelete on write, TTL backstopWrite-through updateUpdating races: two writers can land their cache updates in the opposite order to their database writes and leave the cache permanently stale. Delete has no such race. Ch 9
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Single node dies
Its ~0.5% of keys become misses and are refilled from the origin on demand. Clients mark the node down after a short failure-detection window and skip it on the ring. Critically, the origin must have headroom for a 0.5% miss-rate increase -- which it does, because that is a rounding error against the normal miss rate.
Node flapping
Far worse than a clean death: each transition reshuffles key ownership, so keys ping-pong between nodes and the effective hit rate collapses while both copies go stale. Damp it -- require N consecutive failures to eject and a longer, hysteretic interval to re-admit. Slow, stable membership beats accurate, twitchy membership. Ch 1
Whole cache tier restarts
The genuine disaster: hit rate goes to 0% and the origin sees 20-100x its normal load, which is a metastable failure it will not recover from on its own. Mitigate with staggered restarts (never more than 10% of the fleet at once), a concurrency limit on origin fill so the cache cannot forward more than the origin can serve, and load shedding beyond it. Ch 10
Hot key saturates one node's NIC
Count-min sketch detects the key, the control plane promotes it to replicated + client-L1 mode automatically. Detection must be automatic: by the time a human has read the graph, the node has been dropping packets for ten minutes.
Ring disagreement between clients
During a config rollout, two clients may briefly hold different rings and write the same key to different nodes -- producing two divergent copies with no reconciliation. TTLs bound the damage, and the config service versions the ring so a client can detect and refuse a stale topology. This is why membership is the one thing that gets consensus.

Design Typeahead / Autocomplete (Search Suggestions at Google Scale)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
[list] 1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Given a prefix, return the top 10 completions ranked by likelihood
  • Fire on every keystroke; a 20-character query means up to 20 requests
  • Trending terms must appear within minutes, not days
  • Tolerate typos in the prefix; suppress offensive and unsafe suggestions

Non-Functional:

  • p99 under 100 ms end to end — above roughly 100 ms the suggestion arrives after the user has typed the next character, and the feature stops feeling live
  • Read-dominated to an extreme degree: essentially 100% reads on the serving path
  • Stale suggestions are acceptable; slow suggestions are not
💡 The reframe that carries the interview

This is not a search problem, it is a precomputation problem. You are not searching a corpus at request time — you are looking up an answer that was computed hours ago. Once you say that, every subsequent decision follows: the serving path does one lookup and no ranking, and all the interesting engineering moves offline into the pipeline that builds the lookup table.

[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation

Assumptions: 5B searches/day; ~15 keystroke requests per search after client-side debouncing; 100M distinct queries worth suggesting.

~75B
suggestion reqs/day
~870K
QPS average
~2.6M
QPS peak (3x)
~500M
distinct prefixes
~150 GB
prefix→top10 table
<100 ms
p99 budget

The estimate that decides the architecture: 500M prefixes × 10 suggestions × ~30 bytes ≈ 150 GB. That fits in the RAM of a modest cluster — perhaps 8 machines with replication. The entire answer set fits in memory, which is why the serving path can be a hash lookup and why p99 under 100 ms is comfortably achievable.

Note the client-side saving: debouncing at ~50 ms and cancelling in-flight requests cuts request volume by roughly 60% for free, before any server-side work. Mention it — the cheapest capacity is the request you never send.

[plug] 3. API Design
GET /v1/suggest?q={prefix}&lang=&country=&n=10 Response: 200 { suggestions:[{ text, score, type }], ttl_ms } Headers: Cache-Control: private, max-age=60 Errors: returns 200 with [] -- NEVER an error. // A failed suggestion must look like "no suggestions", // never like a broken page. Fail invisibly. // Transport: keep-alive HTTP/2 or a persistent WebSocket. TCP+TLS // setup per keystroke would blow the entire latency budget. POST /v1/feedback // which suggestion was accepted Body: { prefix, shown[], selected_index, session } // This is the training signal that ranks tomorrow's table.
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- SERVING: a flat, immutable, precomputed map. No tree walk at read time. TABLE prefix_top_k { prefix VARCHAR(1..20) PRIMARY KEY, -- + lang, country suggestions BLOB -- packed [text, score] x 10 } -- Built offline. Served from RAM. Sharded by hash(prefix). -- OFFLINE: the trie exists only in the build pipeline, never at read time. NODE trie_node { children MAP<char, node>, top_k ARRAY[10] -- cached at EVERY node } -- Caching top_k at each node is the whole trick: it converts -- "walk the subtree and rank" into "read one array". TABLE query_counts { -- the ranking input query, lang, country, count_7d, count_1h, ctr, is_safe }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
OFFLINE PIPELINE (hourly) SERVING PATH (per keystroke) query logs (last 7d) browser | | debounce 50ms, v | cancel in-flight aggregate + filter v (safety, spam, PII) CDN / edge cache | | ~40% hit on v | common prefixes build TRIE, cache top-k v at every node SUGGEST SERVICE | | hash(prefix) -> shard v v flatten -> prefix_top_k IN-MEMORY SHARDS | one hash lookup, no ranking v | ATOMIC SWAP into serving -------------------+ (version the whole table; flip a pointer. Never mutate in place -- a half-updated table serves incoherent suggestions.) REAL-TIME LANE (minutes): trending terms from a streaming count-min sketch, merged at read time as a small overlay on top of the hourly table.
Two lanes, deliberately. The hourly batch lane gives quality and safety review; the streaming lane gives freshness for breaking terms. Merging a small overlay at read time is far cheaper than rebuilding 150 GB every minute.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Why not walk a trie at request time? A trie find-the-prefix is O(len), which is fine — but then you must traverse the entire subtree beneath it to collect and rank candidates. For the prefix “a” that subtree is essentially the whole corpus. Caching the top 10 at every node converts that traversal into a single array read, and it is the difference between a system that works and one that times out on the first character. The cost is memory and rebuild time, both of which you have.

Sharding: by prefix, not by node. Hash the prefix string and shard on that, so any single request is answered by exactly one shard with no scatter-gather. Sharding the trie structurally — by first letter, say — is the trap: it produces wildly unequal shards (far more queries start with s than with z) and forces multi-shard traversal. Replicate the entire table to every serving node instead if it fits, which at 150 GB it nearly does; full replication makes every node able to answer everything and eliminates the routing problem outright. Ch 5

The short-prefix problem. Single-character prefixes are requested orders of magnitude more often than long ones. These are perfect cache candidates precisely because they are both hottest and most stable — the top suggestions for “a” barely move hour to hour. Push the first two characters' worth of results to the CDN and the client, and a large fraction of traffic never reaches your service at all.

Typo tolerance without paying for it on every request. Full edit-distance search over the trie at request time is too slow. Instead, precompute: for known high-frequency misspellings, store the corrected prefix's results directly under the misspelling as an ordinary key. This turns fuzzy matching into an exact lookup and costs only offline build time. Reserve genuine edit-distance search for the tail, behind a stricter latency budget, and only when the exact lookup returned nothing.

Ranking is where the product lives. Raw frequency is a weak signal because it is dominated by yesterday's news and never surfaces anything rising. Blend: 7-day frequency for stability, 1-hour frequency for trend, historical click-through rate for quality, plus personalisation and locale. Then apply the safety filter last and hard — suggestion lists are published editorial content, and an offensive completion is a public incident, not a relevance bug. The safety filter must run at build time and again at serve time, because the streaming overlay bypasses the batch review.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Read pathPrecomputed prefix→top10 mapLive trie traversalTraversing the subtree under a one-character prefix means ranking the whole corpus. Precomputation moves all the work offline, where it has hours instead of milliseconds.
ShardingHash of prefix (or full replication)By first letterStructural sharding produces grossly unequal shards and multi-shard reads. At 150 GB, replicating everything to every node is both affordable and simpler.
FreshnessHourly batch + streaming overlayContinuous rebuildRebuilding 150 GB per minute is enormous waste for a handful of changed entries. A small merged overlay gets the freshness at a fraction of the cost.
TyposPrecomputed misspelling keysEdit distance at query timeFuzzy search over a large trie cannot fit a 100 ms budget. Precomputing the common cases converts it to an exact lookup; the long tail is not worth the latency.
On failureReturn empty, 200 OK5xx errorAutocomplete is an enhancement. Degrading to "no suggestions" is invisible; an error is a visible broken feature. Never let an optional component fail loudly.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Build pipeline fails
Keep serving the previous table version indefinitely. Suggestions age gracefully -- a day-old table is barely distinguishable to users -- so there is never a reason to swap in a partial build. Alert on table age, not on job failure, because a job that "succeeded" with 3% of the data is the more dangerous outcome.
Bad table published
Versioned tables and a pointer swap make rollback a single atomic flip. Gate the swap on automated checks: table size within 10% of the previous build, top suggestions for a fixed set of canary prefixes unchanged beyond a threshold, and zero safety-filter violations in a sampled scan.
Serving shard dies
Data is immutable and fully replicated, so any surviving replica answers identically -- no rebuild, no repartition, no state to recover. This is the payoff for making the serving tier stateless over a read-only snapshot: node failure is a routing event, not a data event.
Traffic spike (breaking news)
The spike concentrates on a few prefixes, which is the best possible shape for a cache -- CDN and client caching absorb the bulk of it. Beyond that, shed load by shortening result lists and raising client debounce via a server-pushed config, degrading quality before availability.
Offensive suggestion surfaces
Blocklist evaluated at build AND serve time, because the streaming overlay skips the batch review path. Serve-time filtering also gives a same-minute kill switch for a specific term without waiting for a rebuild -- which is the response time this class of incident actually requires.

Design a RAG Q&A System (Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Private Data)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Answer natural-language questions over a customer's private document corpus (10M documents, ~50 GB of text)
  • Every answer carries citations to the source passages it used
  • Respect per-user access control — a user must never see content from a document they cannot open
  • New and updated documents become answerable within 15 minutes

Non-Functional:

  • p95 under 3 seconds to first token; streaming thereafter
  • Cost per query is a first-class constraint, not an afterthought
  • Answers must be attributable; “I don't know” is a correct and required output
💡 Two things to say early that most candidates miss

First: this is two systems — an offline indexing pipeline and an online serving path — and almost all the quality lives in the offline half while all the latency lives in the online half. Second: access control must be enforced at retrieval time, not by filtering the answer. Once a restricted passage enters the prompt, the model may paraphrase it and no downstream filter can reliably catch that. Post-filtering a generated answer is not a security control.

[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation

Assumptions: 10M documents averaging 5 KB of text; chunked at ~500 tokens with overlap; 1,536-dimension embeddings; 100K queries/day.

~100M
chunks
6 KB
per vector (fp32)
~600 GB
vectors, unquantised
~150 GB
int8 quantised
~1.2
QPS average
~4K
prompt tokens/query

The number that reframes the problem: 1.2 QPS is nothing. This system is not throughput-constrained — it is cost- and quality-constrained. Say that explicitly, because it inverts the usual instinct: the interesting engineering here is not sharding for scale, it is the index that fits in memory and the tokens you do not send.

Vector index sizing is the real capacity question. 600 GB of fp32 vectors does not fit one machine; 150 GB of int8 does, comfortably. Scalar quantisation to int8 costs a few percent of recall and 4× the memory — the single highest-leverage trade in the design. Note also that an HNSW graph adds roughly 30–50% overhead on top of the vectors for its edge lists.

Cost: at ~4K prompt tokens per query, token spend dominates everything else. Trimming retrieved context from 10 chunks to 5 nearly halves the bill and frequently improves answer quality.

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /v1/ask Body: { question, conversation_id?, filters{}, stream:true } Auth: user token -> resolved to an ACL group set Response: server-sent events { type:"retrieval", chunks:[{doc_id, score, snippet}] } { type:"token", text:"..." } // streamed { type:"citation", span:[s,e], doc_id, chunk_id } { type:"done", usage:{prompt_tokens, completion_tokens} } Errors: 422 no_relevant_context // retrieval found nothing 429 token_budget_exceeded // Emitting the retrieval event FIRST is a real design decision: the // user sees sources in ~300ms while generation runs, which makes a // 3-second answer feel responsive and makes the system auditable. POST /v1/documents // triggers async re-index POST /v1/feedback // thumbs + which citation was wrong
[db] 4. Schema Design
TABLE chunks { chunk_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, doc_id UUID, ordinal INT, -- position within the document text TEXT, -- the chunk itself heading_path TEXT, -- "Handbook > Leave > Parental" acl_groups ARRAY<UUID>, -- DENORMALISED from the document embedding VECTOR(1536), content_hash BYTES, -- skip re-embedding unchanged chunks updated_at TIMESTAMP } -- acl_groups is denormalised ON PURPOSE. The ANN index must filter -- during the graph walk; a post-hoc join cannot -- you would retrieve -- 10 results, discard 9 for permissions, and return almost nothing. -- Two indexes over the same chunks, queried together: -- HNSW over embedding (semantic / meaning) -- BM25 inverted over text (lexical / exact terms, IDs, error codes)
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
OFFLINE: INDEXING ONLINE: SERVING document source user question + auth | | v v parse + extract rewrite query (PDF, HTML, tables) (resolve "it", "that one", | expand acronyms) v | CHUNK ~500 tokens, +-----------+-----------+ 15% overlap, never v v across a heading VECTOR SEARCH BM25 SEARCH | HNSW, ACL-filtered lexical, exact v during graph walk terms and IDs EMBED (batched, skip | | unchanged content_hash) +-----------+-----------+ | v v FUSE (reciprocal rank) write vectors + BM25 top ~50 candidates + acl_groups | | v v RERANK cross-encoder ATOMIC INDEX SWAP 50 -> top 5 | v ASSEMBLE PROMPT -> LLM stream tokens + citations Two retrievers, then rerank. Vector search finds meaning; BM25 finds the exact error code or product name that embeddings routinely miss. Neither alone is enough.
The retrieve-wide-then-rerank-narrow shape is the core pattern: cheap recall over 50 candidates, then an expensive, accurate model over only those 50. Sending all 50 to the LLM would cost 10× as much and answer worse.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Chunking is the highest-leverage decision and the one most often rushed. Chunk too small and you sever the context that makes a passage meaningful; too large and the embedding averages several topics into a vector that matches none of them well. Split on document structure — headings, sections, paragraph boundaries — never on a fixed character count that cuts mid-sentence. Overlap adjacent chunks by 10–15% so a fact spanning a boundary survives in at least one. And prepend the heading path to each chunk's text before embedding: a chunk reading “employees receive 12 weeks” is nearly useless in isolation, and decisive when it begins “Handbook > Leave > Parental”.

Why hybrid retrieval, concretely. Embeddings capture semantic similarity and are systematically bad at rare exact tokens — an error code like ERR_4021, a part number, an unusual surname. BM25 handles those and is helpless at paraphrase. Run both, then fuse with reciprocal rank fusion, which combines by rank position rather than by score and so needs no score normalisation between two incomparable scoring systems. This is a small amount of work for a large and reliable quality gain.

Access control must filter inside the ANN search. HNSW navigates a proximity graph; if you filter results after the walk, you may traverse to 10 neighbours and discard 9 for permissions, returning one weak result while better permitted chunks sat one hop away unexplored. The index must evaluate the ACL predicate during traversal so the walk keeps expanding until it has 10 permitted results. This is why acl_groups is denormalised onto the chunk — and it is the detail that separates a demo from a system you can sell to an enterprise.

Attributing failure — the question a good interviewer will ask. When an answer is wrong, was it retrieval or generation? These have opposite fixes, so you must be able to tell them apart. Instrument both: log the retrieved chunks with every answer, and evaluate them separately — retrieval by whether the passage containing the answer was in the top k on a labelled set, generation by whether the answer is supported by the passages actually supplied. A retrieval failure means fixing chunking, embeddings or the reranker; a generation failure means fixing the prompt or the model. Teams that measure only end-to-end accuracy cannot act on the number they have.

Cost and latency levers, in order of value: cache embeddings by content_hash so re-indexing an edited document re-embeds only changed chunks; cache whole answers for repeated questions, which in an enterprise corpus is a surprisingly large fraction; trim to 5 reranked chunks rather than 10; and stream tokens so time-to-first-token is what the user experiences rather than total generation time.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
RetrievalHybrid vector + BM25, fusedVector onlyEmbeddings systematically miss rare exact tokens -- error codes, part numbers, names -- which are exactly what users paste into a search box. Cheap to add, large and reliable quality gain.
Vector storageint8 scalar quantisationfp324x memory reduction for a few percent of recall. Turns a 600 GB multi-machine index into a 150 GB single-machine one, which removes an entire distribution problem.
Access controlFilter during ANN traversalPost-filter resultsPost-filtering returns too few results and, worse, is not a security boundary: once a restricted passage is in the prompt the model can paraphrase it past any output filter.
RerankingCross-encoder over top 50Send all 50 to the LLM10x the token cost for worse answers -- long contexts dilute attention and degrade quality. Retrieve wide, rerank, then send narrow.
FreshnessIncremental by content_hashNightly full re-indexRe-embedding 100M unchanged chunks nightly is enormous waste and cannot meet a 15-minute freshness target.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Retrieval returns nothing relevant
Threshold on the reranker score and return an explicit "I could not find this in your documents" rather than generating from the model's parametric memory. An unsupported answer that looks confident is worse than no answer, because the user cannot tell the difference -- and this is the single most damaging failure mode of the whole class of system.
LLM provider slow or unavailable
Timeout and fall back to returning the retrieved passages with highlights -- degraded to search, but still useful, and still cited. Circuit-break on sustained failure rather than queueing requests that will time out anyway. Ch 10
Vector index corrupt or mid-rebuild
Build into a new index version and swap atomically; never mutate the serving index in place. Keep the previous version on disk for instant rollback. Until the swap, BM25 alone still answers -- degraded recall on paraphrase, but the system stays up.
Document permissions change
This is a correctness AND security issue: revocation must propagate faster than re-indexing. Resolve ACLs at query time against the live permission service for the candidate set, using the denormalised acl_groups only as a pre-filter. Slightly slower, and it means a revoked user stops seeing content within seconds rather than at the next index build.
Prompt injection from document content
Retrieved chunks are untrusted input, not instructions -- a document containing "ignore previous instructions" must not be obeyed. Keep retrieved content in a clearly delimited region of the prompt, instruct the model to treat it as data, and validate that emitted citations actually point at retrieved chunks. Treat this as an injection class alongside SQL injection, not as an AI curiosity. Ch 15
Part 3
Google Staff (L6) Interview Framework & Master Toolkit
Strategic execution guides, capacity estimation mental math, trade-off matrices, and behavioral leadership frameworks calibrated specifically for Staff Software Engineer evaluations at top-tier tech companies (Google L6, Meta E6, Amazon L7).

1. The 45-Minute Staff (L6) System Design Pacing Guide

At Google L6, the interviewer does not want to prompt you. They expect you to own the room, proactively drive the architecture, state assumptions clearly, and pivot between high-level macro trade-offs and micro-level algorithmic deep dives.

Time Phase Staff-Level Execution Strategy What Interviewers Evaluate
0:00 - 0:05 Scope & Requirements Clarify core Functional Requirements (3-4 max). Define crisp Non-Functional SLAs (Availability 99.99%, latency targets p99 < 50ms, data durability). State explicit out-of-scope items. Ability to ruthlessly prioritize and avoid over-engineering trivial features.
0:05 - 0:10 Capacity Estimation Calculate DAU, write QPS, read QPS, network ingress/egress bandwidth, and 5-year storage requirements. Convert storage into hardware count (RAM vs NVMe vs Object Store). Practical engineering instinct; grounding architectural decisions in hardware physics.
0:10 - 0:18 High-Level Architecture Sketch end-to-end data flow: Client -> DNS/CDN -> Load Balancer -> API Gateway -> Microservices -> Message Queues -> Primary/Replica DB & Cache. Establish data contracts (APIs). Breadth of knowledge; clean separation of concerns and clear system boundaries.
0:18 - 0:35 Deep Dives & Hard Problems Dive deep into the 2-3 most technically complex bottlenecks (e.g. Celebrity fan-out, cross-DC consensus, exactly-once transactions, geospatial matching, data synchronization). The Core L6 Differentiator: Depth in distributed algorithms, concurrency, and DB internals.
0:35 - 0:42 Fault Tolerance & Bottlenecks Walk through failure modes: "What if the Redis master crashes?", "What if a network partition isolates Region B?", "How do we handle a thundering herd during Super Bowl?". Resilience thinking, self-correction, graceful degradation, and operational excellence.
0:42 - 0:45 Summary & Extensibility Summarize the system's operational guarantees. Proactively mention future scale enhancements (e.g. machine learning rankers, cost optimizations). Executive communication and holistic strategic vision.

2. Latency Numbers & Capacity Mental Math Every Staff Engineer Must Know

Jeff Dean's latency numbers adjusted for modern hardware (NVMe SSDs, 100GbE data center networks, cloud infrastructure):

0.5 ns
L1 CPU Cache Reference
10 ns
L3 CPU Cache Reference
100 ns
Main Memory (DRAM) Reference
10 μs
NVMe SSD Random Read
0.5 ms
Intra-Data Center RTT
10 ms
Rotational Disk (HDD) Seek
70 ms
Cross-Continent RTT (US East -> Europe)
150 ms
Transpacific RTT (US West -> Asia)

Rule-of-Thumb Conversion Factors:

  • Seconds in a day: 86,400 ≈ 100,000 (makes mental math 10x faster: 10M requests/day ≈ 100 QPS; 1 Billion requests/day ≈ 10,000 QPS).
  • Storage conversions: 1 Million records × 1 KB = 1 GB; 1 Billion records × 1 KB = 1 TB; 1 Billion records × 1 MB = 1 PB.
  • Network throughput: 1 Gbps link ≈ 125 MB/sec; 10 Gbps link ≈ 1.25 GB/sec.
  • Redis throughput: Single thread Redis node ≈ 50,000 - 100,000 QPS. Cluster of 10 nodes handles ~1M QPS easily.
  • Postgres / MySQL throughput: Single primary handles ≈ 5,000 - 10,000 writes/sec (with SSD WAL); Read replicas handle ~20,000 - 50,000 reads/sec each.

3. The Grand Architecture Trade-off Matrix

Staff engineers never say "Technology X is the best." They say: "Under constraints A and B, Technology X is superior because of trade-off Y."

Architectural Decision Option A Option B Staff-Level Decision Rule
Data Model Relational (PostgreSQL, Spanner) NoSQL / Document (Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB) Use Relational when you need complex JOINs, ACID guarantees, or schema evolution. Use NoSQL when you need petabyte-scale horizontal writes, simple key-based access patterns, and schema flexibility.
Data Ingestion Synchronous RPC (gRPC / REST) Asynchronous Messaging (Kafka / SQS / PubSub) Use Sync RPC when the client strictly needs the immediate return value to continue (e.g. Auth, Checkout validation). Use Message Queues for fire-and-forget, buffering high spikes, and decoupling consumer systems.
Client Push Protocol WebSockets Server-Sent Events (SSE) / HTTP Long-Polling Use WebSockets for bidirectional real-time communication (Chat, Collaborative Whiteboards, Multiplayer Games). Use SSE for unidirectional server-to-client streaming (AI text generation, live stock ticker).
Cache Invalidation Write-Through Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) Use Write-Through when read latency must always be minimal (zero cache miss penalty) and data cannot tolerate staleness. Use Cache-Aside when write volume is high and only a fraction of data is frequently read.
Distributed Transactions Two-Phase Commit (2PC) Saga Pattern (Choreographed / Orchestrated) Use 2PC within homogeneous, low-latency NewSQL clusters (Spanner). Use Sagas across disparate microservices where long-running locks are intolerable and compensating actions are feasible.
Search Indexing Elasticsearch / OpenSearch PostgreSQL Full-Text Search (GIN Index) Use Postgres FTS when data volume is < 10M rows and you want zero operational overhead. Use Elasticsearch when you need fuzzy matching, typo tolerance, multi-faceted filtering, and scale across billions of documents.

4. Google L6 Staff Leadership & Engineering Scenarios

In Google Staff interviews (System Design & Leadership / Googlyness), evaluators look for specific L6 behaviors: driving consensus among conflicting senior engineers, managing technical debt vs velocity, preventing catastrophic post-mortems, and designing scalable organizational architectures.

How do you handle two Principal Engineers with opposing architectural visions?
Staff Answer Strategy: "I do not arbitrate based on seniority or debate in endless meetings. I establish a shared Decision Framework based on business constraints (Latency SLA, operational cost, team ramp-up time). I ask each engineer to write a 1-page design proposal addressing the matrix, run a time-boxed 3-day proof of concept (POC) benchmarking the critical path under synthetic load, and align the team around empirical data. If trade-offs remain evenly matched, I favor reversible decisions (Type 2) over irreversible ones (Type 1) and establish a clear escalation path."
Describe how you lead a high-severity (SEV-0) cascading outage post-mortem.
Staff Answer Strategy: "I enforce a Blameless Post-Mortem culture focused on systemic prevention. I lead the investigation using the '5 Whys' root-cause methodology. We isolate why the blast radius was not contained (e.g. missing circuit breaker, lack of load shedding, synchronous dependency cycles). I convert learnings into concrete P0 Action Items with assigned owners: adding deadline propagation, automated canary analysis (ACA), chaos engineering drills, and updating playbooks before declaring the post-mortem closed."
How do you manage massive technical debt that threatens system scalability?
Staff Answer Strategy: "I never ask product management for a '6-month complete rewrite'—that almost always fails. Instead, I quantify the business risk of technical debt (e.g. 'each release carries a 15% rollback rate and infrastructure costs grow super-linearly with user growth'). I use the Strangler Fig Pattern: progressively decomposing the legacy monolith by routing 1% -> 5% -> 100% of traffic to isolated microservices behind an API gateway, delivering incremental value while reducing operational risk."

5. The Mental Model — How All of This Fits Together

Fifteen chapters is a lot of parts. This is the single diagram that connects them. Read it top to bottom: each layer's decisions are constrained by the layer above, and the bottom half exists only because the physical world refuses to cooperate.

REQUIREMENTS │ what are we actually being asked to build? ▼ WORKLOAD & SLOs ← Ch 1, 14 load parameters (usually a DISTRIBUTION, not an average) percentiles, not means │ what must never break ▼ DATA MODEL ← Ch 12 relationship shape picks relational / document / graph ▼ STORAGE ENGINE ← Ch 12 B-tree vs LSM — decided by the read/write ratio above │ ┌───────── ONE MACHINE IS NO LONGER ENOUGH ────────┐ ▼ REPLICATION ↔↔↔ PARTITIONING ← Ch 4, 5 SAME data, DIFFERENT data, many nodes different nodes → availability → capacity → read scale → write scale ▼ ORTHOGONAL. Composed, not sequenced. The hard problems live in their INTERACTION. ▼ TRANSACTIONS ← Ch 7 the guarantee you WANT across all of that ▼ ######################################################### # THE TROUBLE WITH DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS ← Ch 1, 8 # # asynchronous network + lying clocks + pauses # # # # ⇒ you cannot tell "slow" from "dead" # # ⇒ every guarantee above is now an ASSUMPTION # ######################################################### ▼ CONSISTENCY & CONSENSUS ← Ch 2, 3, 6 the PRICE LIST │ linearizability → costs latency, always, not just in partitions │ causality → the strongest model that stays fast + available │ total order broadcast ≡ consensus ≡ leader election ≡ linearizable compare-and-set ▼ "Buy the MINIMUM coordination that makes your invariant hold."
💡 The three relationships people miss

1. Replication and partitioning are orthogonal, and their interaction is where the hard problems are. Rebalancing a shard that has three replicas; global vs local secondary indexes; routing a request when both the partition map and the leader can change. Neither chapter alone prepares you for those.

2. The “trouble” layer is a refutation, not a list of war stories. Read it as: everything above assumed you can tell whether a node is alive. You cannot. Fencing tokens are the punchline — the lease you thought you held may have expired during a GC pause, and only the storage layer rejecting a stale token saves you.

3. The bottom line is an equivalence, not four definitions. Once you see that total order broadcast, consensus, leader election and linearizable compare-and-set are one problem, “do we need consensus here?” becomes answerable: you need it exactly when you need a total order, and you need a total order exactly when an invariant spans nodes.

When You See This in a Design Problem, Think This

The point of the guide is that when you meet an unfamiliar problem, you recognise its shape. This is the lookup table.

When the problem says…The real question is…Reach for
“must never lose data”What is the acceptable RPO, and against which failure?Sync replication, WAL + fsync, quorum writes Ch 4, 12
“high write throughput”Are the writes random or can they be sequential?LSM, partitioning, batching, log-structured design Ch 5, 12
“globally distributed”Which operations must cross regions? Speed of light is 150ms.Geo-partitioned ownership, causal consistency, follower reads Ch 4, 2
“booking / reservation / seats”Is this a phantom? Can the invariant live on one row?Materialize the conflict, or SERIALIZABLE + retry Ch 7
“must be unique globally”Uniqueness, or ordering? They are different.Unique constraint if single-leader; consensus if sharded. IDs need neither — use disjoint ranges Ch 6
“exactly once”Exactly-once delivery is impossible. Do you mean effect?At-least-once + idempotency key + dedupe store Ch 1, 15
“social feed / timeline”Fan-out on write or read? What about celebrities?Hybrid fan-out; a timeline is a materialized view Ch 11, 12
“real-time / live updates”Server → client only, or bidirectional?SSE if one-way; WebSocket + pub/sub backplane if not Ch 11
“search / filter by anything”Is the filter the partition key? If not, you are scattering.Local index + scatter/gather, or a CDC-fed search store Ch 5, 12
“analytics on live data”OLTP and OLAP are opposite machines.CDC into a columnar store. Never the OLTP primary Ch 12
“run exactly once per hour”The lock is not enough — pauses outlive leases.Consensus election + fencing token + idempotent job Ch 6, 8
“across multiple services”Can I redraw the boundary so it becomes local?First try co-location. Then saga + outbox. Never 2PC Ch 7, 13
“one customer is huge”Hot key. More shards will not help.Salt, tier, or isolate into a dedicated cell Ch 5
“update DB and notify others”That is a dual write — it will drift.Transactional outbox, or CDC off the WAL Ch 13
“p99 is fine but users complain”Where are you measuring, and over what population?Client-side SLI, slice by tenant, fan-out amplification Ch 14
“deploy without downtime”Old and new run together — and rollback must work.Expand/contract, forward compatibility, field numbers Ch 15
“survive a region failure”What is the RTO, and how do clients reconverge?Geo-replication, fencing, rehearsed failover Ch 4
“one slow dependency broke everything”Shared resource pool + retries = cascade.Bulkhead, circuit breaker, retry budget, deadline propagation Ch 13

Twenty Design Mistakes Caused by Misunderstanding This Material

Each of these is a real, recurring failure — and each traces to a specific misconception in the chapters above.

⚠ The recurring twenty
1. Retrying without idempotency
A timeout does not mean it did not happen. Double charges. Ch 1
2. “We're ACID so we're safe”
Default isolation permits write skew. Name your level. Ch 7
3. SELECT FOR UPDATE on absence
You cannot lock rows that do not exist. Phantoms get through. Ch 7
4. W+R>N called “strong”
A probability dial, not a guarantee. Sloppy quorums void it. Ch 4
5. Distributed lock without fencing
A paused holder still writes. Enforce at the resource. Ch 8
6. Auto-failover on async replication
A silent decision to lose acknowledged writes. Ch 4
7. Partitioning by timestamp
100% of writes hit the newest partition. Ch 5
8. More shards to fix a hot key
The hot value hashes to one place regardless. Ch 5
9. Dual-writing DB + cache/index
Guaranteed drift. Use outbox or CDC. Ch 13
10. 2PC across microservices
Blocking, and availability is the product of all participants. Ch 7
11. Application data in etcd/ZK
Coordination services, not databases. A known way to kill a cluster. Ch 6
12. Dependency checks in liveness probes
One DB blip restarts the whole fleet. Ch 13
13. Retries at every layer
3×3×3 = 27× load during an incident. Budget them at one layer. Ch 13
14. Unbounded queues
Converts a throughput problem into an OOM. Bound every queue. Ch 13
15. Averaging latency
Describes nobody. And percentiles do not average either. Ch 14
16. LWW on wall clocks
Clock skew silently discards correct writes. Ch 8
17. Analytics on the OLTP primary
Buffer-pool eviction, I/O contention, blocked vacuum. Ch 12
18. Renaming a column in one deploy
Breaks un-upgraded nodes and makes rollback impossible. Ch 15
19. Auto-rebalance + auto-failure-detection
A cascading-failure generator. Keep a human in the loop. Ch 5
20. “Eventual consistency is fine”
Unfalsifiable without a number. Measure lag or you have not chosen it. Ch 4
🌱 The six sentences worth memorising
  • You cannot distinguish a slow node from a dead one. Everything else follows from this.
  • A timeout tells you nothing about whether the work happened. So make the work safe to repeat.
  • Do not prevent the stale actor from acting — make its action harmless. Idempotency and fencing are both this.
  • Consensus, total order broadcast, leader election and linearizable CAS are one problem. Buy the minimum.
  • Making a constraint local beats coordinating. Co-locate the data, or move the invariant onto one row.
  • Every guarantee has a price, and the price is usually latency — all the time, not just during failures.

6. What Google Actually Asks — The Question Bank

Every other section of this guide teaches mechanisms. This one is about targeting: which mechanisms you are most likely to be asked to assemble under time pressure, and where in this document the answer already lives. It is built from cross-referencing eight public question banks and candidate reports — read the provenance note at the end before you treat any of it as gospel.

💡 The single fact that should reshape your preparation

At L6 you are preparing for two design rounds, not one. An L5 loop contains a single system design interview. An L6 loop contains two — sometimes three — and they are deliberately different in kind: one product / applied design, and one infrastructure / architecture design.

Almost all popular preparation material is the product round, and this guide originally was too — nine of its first ten designs. D11–D14 and the enrichment of Ch 9 and Ch 10 exist specifically to close that half of the loop. The infra round is the one candidates under-prepare, because it does not look like the questions in the videos.

What the infrastructure round actually looks like

These are real reported prompts, and they are the reason “I have practised Design Twitter” is not sufficient preparation at this level:

  • “How would you upgrade 5,000 servers?”
  • “Design a system to log messages in order.”
  • “Design a metrics and logging service.”
  • “Design a distributed LRU cache.”
  • “Design a system to deny service to requests from banned IPs, from a list published by a third party.”
  • “Design a function that schedules jobs on a rack of machines, where each job needs a certain amount of CPU and RAM and each machine has different amounts of both.”
  • “Design a system to upgrade hundreds of thousands of machines on the Moon.”

Notice what these have in common. There is no user-facing product, no feed, no timeline. They are fleet management, observability and admission control — the problems a company that runs its own planet-scale infrastructure actually has. The last one is not a joke question: it is a latency-constraint question wearing a costume. A 1.3-second one-way light delay makes every synchronous protocol you know unusable, and the interviewer wants to watch you notice that.

Tier 1 — the highest-probability questions

Ranked by how many independent sources report them. The last column is the honest state of this guide.

“Sources” means how many of the eight banks consulted listed it — not measured interview frequency. Treat multi-source rows as solid and single-source rows as weak signal.

Tier 2 — reported, plausible, worth a mental rehearsal

Distributed counter at Google scale · global config / feature-flag service · API gateway at 10M+ rps with throttling and auth · trending hashtags · global ID generation · ad aggregation · real-time leaderboard at Pokémon Go scale · near-duplicate video detection · Street View image ingestion · Drive-style usage quota limiter · calendar event conflict handling · online coding judge · the Glassdoor classic: “a page showing the status of 10M+ users — name, photo, badge, points.”

Most of these are recombinations of things you already have. A distributed counter is partitioning plus the decision to give up read-your-writes. A leaderboard is a counter plus a top-k problem. Trending hashtags is a leaderboard over a sliding window. If you can derive them at the table you do not need to memorise them.

Tier 3 — the 2026 shift

Multiple sources report Google now weaving AI/ML system design into the loop, and the question banks confirm it with live prompts: design an LLM-based Q&A system, design a retrieval-augmented generation system over a customer’s private data, design an ML experiment tracking platform, design serving infrastructure for an LLM under low-latency, high-throughput requirements, design a task scheduler for opaque long-running GPU jobs, design a billing-token rate limiter for AI agents.

This is the fastest-moving part of the loop and the part where the classic canon helps you least. The reassuring half of that: an inference-serving system is a queueing and batching problem, and a RAG pipeline is an indexing and retrieval problem. Both are made of parts this guide already teaches. The unfamiliar half is the vocabulary and the failure modes, which is what D14 is for.

⚠ Common misconception
“The popular list of system design questions is the Google list.”

It substantially is not. The public canon — Twitter, Uber, Netflix, Instagram — is consumer product design, because that is what makes legible video content. Google’s reported pool leans much harder toward infrastructure and operations, because that is the problem domain of a company that runs its own fleet, its own storage layer and its own network.

There is also a selection bias worth naming: preparation vendors publish the questions they already have content for. A question that appears on five prep sites is evidence about the prep market, and only indirectly about Google. Weight candidate reports above vendor lists wherever the two disagree.

The rubric — the same prompt, three different bars

The most consistent finding across every source is that the L4/L5/L6 distinction is not about which mechanisms you know. It is about who speaks first.

THE SAME PROMPT, THREE DIFFERENT BARS L4 the interviewer states the requirements -> the candidate builds to them "here is a design that satisfies what you told me" L5 the candidate surfaces the missing requirements before being asked "you have not mentioned retention -- I will assume 30 days, which is what decides the storage tier" L6 the candidate names the DOMINANT CONSTRAINT before the interviewer steers "everything here is downstream of one number: the 40:1 read/write skew. I am designing around that, and I will justify every other choice against it." ^ at L6 the highest-signal moments of the round are started by the CANDIDATE. An interviewer who has to pull the trade-offs out of you has already written "solid L5" on the feedback form.
The ladder is about initiative, not vocabulary. This is why a clean, correct, well-scaled architecture is one of the most common paths to a down-level: it is a complete answer to a question nobody asked you to answer alone.

That last point deserves stating plainly, because it is counter-intuitive and it is the single most-cited down-level cause: a technically excellent design can read as L5. A clean architecture with sensible trade-offs is a strong L4 result. What converts it into an L6 result is that you decided what the problem was, said which constraint dominates, named what you were deliberately not building, and volunteered the failure modes before anyone asked.

⚠ Where this list comes from, and how much to trust it

None of this is confirmed by Google. It is aggregated from public preparation vendors and crowd-reported candidate experiences, both of which have known biases: vendors list what they sell content for, and candidates disproportionately report the questions they found memorable or difficult. Two sources I wanted were unreachable, so the first-hand candidate layer here is thinner than the vendor layer.

Use it to allocate study time, not to predict your loop. The value of the tiering is that it tells you where the infrastructure round lives — and that finding is robust across every source, even where individual questions are not.

🌱 Takeaway — how to use this bank

Do not grind the list. Fifteen memorised designs lose to four derivable ones.

  • Prepare two rounds, split by kind. One product, one infrastructure. If your practice is all product designs, half your loop is unrehearsed.
  • The infra round is fleet, observability and admission control. Upgrading a fleet, ordering a log, capping a caller, caching at scale — not feeds.
  • Derive rather than memorise. Counter → leaderboard → trending topics is one problem with three coats of paint. So is crawler → indexer → typeahead.
  • Say the dominant constraint out loud in the first five minutes. It is the cheapest available L6 signal and most candidates never spend it.
  • Volunteer the failure modes. If the interviewer has to ask “what happens when that node dies”, you have already handed away the point.
  • Budget time for the end. The highest-signal discussion is late-round trade-offs and failure analysis. Candidates who over-invest in the first architecture diagram never reach it.
